title: Day 25 — practise the complete workflow
section: Station 2 — repair a small R analysis
text:
Station 2 — repair a small R analysis
The following is deliberately broken code shown as text. Do not copy it into a working report unchanged. Find at least three problems, then write a corrected version in recovery.R in your project root:
seedling <- read_csv("seedlings.csv")
seedlings <- mutate(seedlings, growth_mm = final_mm + initial_mm)
mean(seedlings$Growth_mm)
Consider package loading, file location, object names, case, and the meaning of growth. Confirm the repaired calculation using P01: initial length 25.7 mm, final length 44.3 mm. Save a labelled plot without changing raw data.






A working repair





library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
seedlings <- seedlings |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
mean(seedlings$growth_mm)
P01 grew 18.6 mm. The original used a wrong relative path, inconsistent object names, addition rather than subtraction, and inconsistent column case. It also did not establish that readr and dplyr were loaded in this session.

title: Day 25 — practise the complete workflow
text:
Station 3 — explain before calculating
Write a sentence responding to each situation. No new test is required.

One treated plant has 100 cells measured; one control plant also has 100. A student says there are 100 independent replicates per group. What is wrong?
Two groups have the same mean but one has twice the SD. What can you say about their observations?
A missing biomass value is replaced with zero. Why can that change the biological meaning of the analysis?
A treatment-minus-control estimate is 3 mm with a 95% interval of −2 to 8 mm. Does this establish no effect?
An unknown sample gives absorbance greater than the largest calibration standard. What should happen before reporting its concentration?
A fitted leaf-area/mass slope is positive. Does it prove that changing area experimentally will produce the same change in mass?







Compare your reasoning






There is only one independent treated and one independent control plant; cells within them do not supply independent treatment allocation.
Spread differs even though the means match. Equal means do not imply identical observations or distributions.
Unknown biomass and genuinely absent biomass are different observations. Zero invents a value and can shift the mean, SD, and comparison.
No: the interval includes zero and effects in both directions. Explain the range of compatible values rather than declaring equality.
Flag it as beyond range; dilute and remeasure using the assay protocol.
No: this is an observational association. Other plant properties may vary too.

title: Day 23 — plan and analyse a small biological study
text:
Duckweed is a small aquatic plant that grows as floating fronds. In our simulated study, twenty separate flasks started with equal amounts of duckweed. Ten flasks were randomly allocated additional nutrients; ten were controls. Final dry biomass was measured after seven days. How does biomass differ between the two allocations, and how uncertain is that estimated difference?
This is guided practice, not an additional examination. Use the workflow you already know with a new dataset. Your deliverable is duckweed-report.Rmd, saved in the project root, and its rendered HTML. Keep the original CSV intact.
Complete one study, not two: use the duckweed study below, or choose the organic-laboratory alternative at the end of this page if your teacher selects that context. The alternative uses the same import/check/plot/report workflow and ends with a descriptive comparison; no new chemistry knowledge or test is required. It does not replace the guided statistical practice in week 4.

title: Day 23 — plan and analyse a small biological study
section: 1. Read the design before the numbers
text:
1. Read the design before the numbers
Open the data dictionary, then locate data/duckweed.csv. The columns are flask_id, treatment, and biomass_mg. The two allocation labels are control and nutrient. One nutrient flask, F17, was spilled before weighing, so its final biomass is unavailable.
In a few sentences, state the question, independent experimental unit, outcome and units, and what happened to F17. Fronds in one flask share their environment; counting them as separate independent replicates would misrepresent the design.
Before analysis, predict the kind of output needed: a plot showing flasks, a summary by group, and an estimate of nutrient minus control mean biomass with its confidence interval. You are not trying to make a p-value small.

title: Day 23 — plan and analyse a small biological study
section: 2. Make a report that runs from its own code
text:
2. Make a report that runs from its own code
Copy the starter report.Rmd using Save As, naming the copy duckweed-report.Rmd in the same project root. Replace the title and biological description. Remove seedling-specific chunks and interpretations before adding duckweed code. Load the same three packages in the setup chunk.
Begin with an import and inspection:
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
duckweed <- read_csv("data/duckweed.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
glimpse(duckweed)
Check row count, distinct identifiers, group labels, missing measurements, and the plausible range of biomass. Record checks as evidence, not simply “the data were checked”. Do not change the missing F17 value to zero or delete the entire row from your original input.






Hint: count missing and available measurements





Within group_by(treatment), use summarise() with n(), sum(!is.na(biomass_mg)), and sum(is.na(biomass_mg)). The number of rows and the number of usable measurements are different here. Use na.rm = TRUE for the mean and SD, while still reporting the missing count.

title: Day 23 — plan and analyse a small biological study
text:
3. Make the descriptive result first
Create a group summary with available n, mean, and SD, all clearly labelled. Make a plot of individual biomass measurements by allocation, using only the available measurements for plotted y values. State how many are unavailable in the caption. A separate available object makes the exclusion explicit:
available <- duckweed |>
  filter(!is.na(biomass_mg))
Use the plot to ask whether the groups differ in location, how much overlap there is, and whether an observation needs checking against source records. No source evidence identifies another value as erroneous. Do not remove a value merely because it looks inconvenient.






Hint: adapt a familiar plot





Start with the week 3 individual-point plot. Change the data to available, x to treatment, y to biomass_mg, and the y-axis label to “Dry biomass after seven days (mg)”. Use horizontal jitter only, so vertical positions stay accurate.

title: Day 23 — plan and analyse a small biological study
text:
4. Estimate the difference
Explain why an independent comparison is appropriate and why this is not a paired before/after analysis. Inspect the individual measurements for severe skew or an influential point; seek advice if the simple model appears unsuitable. Use the guided Welch approach from week 4. Extract nutrient and control vectors and give them in that order to t.test() so that the difference is nutrient minus control. The missing F17 measurement is absent from available, not replaced with an invented value.






Hint: preserve the stated comparison direction





nutrient <- available |>
  filter(treatment == "nutrient")
control <- available |>
  filter(treatment == "control")
comparison <- t.test(nutrient$biomass_mg, control$biomass_mg)
comparison
Read the two means and compute their difference explicitly. comparison$conf.int is the confidence interval for the difference in the order used above.

title: Day 23 — plan and analyse a small biological study
text:
5. Write the interpretation before polishing
Use a short paragraph containing the observed direction and size of the difference in mg, the available sample sizes, the confidence interval, and the p-value with an explanation tied to the question. Add a limitation concerning the missing measurement and the conditions of this small simulated experiment.
Distinguish “these observations support a difference under this model” from “nutrients always produce this change in all plants”. If an interval includes zero, report the uncertainty; do not translate it into proof of no effect. Neither outcome needs rescuing by trying other tests.

title: Day 23 — plan and analyse a small biological study
text:
Completion check

Could a reader identify the flask as the independent unit without opening code?
Are measurements missing for 1 flask, with 19 available in total?
Does the plot show observations and units, and explain the missing value?
Does the direction of the reported difference agree with the code and means?
Does every object used in the report originate in its chunks?







Self-check answers that do not depend on your conclusion





There are 20 rows and unique flask IDs. Ten control and nine nutrient flasks have biomass measurements. F17 remains a documented missing value. A positive nutrient-minus-control estimate means greater mean biomass in nutrient flasks. The conclusion still depends on design, assumptions, uncertainty, and context.

title: Day 23 — plan and analyse a small biological study
section: Alternative study: product yield in an organic laboratory
text:
Alternative study: product yield in an organic laboratory
Question: how does the percentage of product collected vary among the supplied runs and between two labelled protocols? Use this study instead of the duckweed report. Save organic-study.Rmd and its HTML at the project root. If you made organic-report.Rmd on day 15, keep that earlier work and use Save As to create organic-study.Rmd for this study.
An organic synthesis is a procedure intended to make a chemical product. For this exercise, the maximum possible product mass, called the theoretical mass, is already supplied; you do not need a reaction equation or to calculate it. Isolated mass is the dry product collected. Assume it is pure solely for this calculation. Define percentage yield by the supplied relationship:
yield (%) = 100 × isolated mass (g) / theoretical mass (g)
The file data/organic-recovery.csv contains 12 simulated independent synthesis runs, six randomly allocated standard and six modified protocol labels. The starting scales differ, so theoretical masses differ. Compare yields in percent, rather than comparing grams without accounting for those scales. All measurements are present. Repeated weighings of one collected product would not create new synthesis runs.
Start from a root-level copy of the template and remove the seedling-specific code and prose. Import and derive the outcome:
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
organic <- read_csv("data/organic-recovery.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
organic <- organic |>
  mutate(yield_percent = 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g)

Check the 12 unique run_id values, six rows per protocol, numeric mass columns, no missing values, and positive theoretical masses. Check Y01 by hand: 0.62 g collected from a supplied 1.00 g maximum gives 62%.
Summarise n, mean, and SD of yield_percent by protocol. Label SD in percentage points, since it describes spread on a percent scale.
Plot individual yields by protocol with horizontal jitter only. Each point is an independent synthesis run. Save one summary CSV and one labelled PNG in output/, using names beginning organic-.
Describe the observed group difference and overlap. Report it in percentage points, defined as the modified mean minus the standard mean. No hypothesis test or confidence interval is required for this descriptive alternative.
Explain why higher yield alone does not establish greater purity, safety, sustainability, or general superiority. The simplified purity assumption is not an experimental verification of purity.
Render in a fresh R session. The report should identify its question, supplied theoretical masses, formula, independent units, units, checks, and limits.







Hint and completion checks for the alternative





Reuse group_by(protocol) and summarise(n = n(), mean_yield_percent = mean(yield_percent), sd_percentage_points = sd(yield_percent), .groups = "drop"). There are six available runs per protocol. The standard mean is about 68.67% and the modified mean about 77.00%, a descriptive difference of 8.33 percentage points. Do not call that an 8.33% relative increase, and do not claim an inferential conclusion from these summaries alone.



Before you finish: save a first rendered report and a note of anything that failed. Tomorrow we will test whether someone else can reproduce it: Day 24.

title: Day 19 — A calibration line
text:
A laboratory instrument gives an absorbance reading, but we want a concentration. We first measure solutions of known concentration, called standards. Can a straight line describe their readings well enough to estimate the concentration of an unknown sample?
This is a common quantitative laboratory workflow. The prepared standards in data/calibration.csv cover 0–10 mg/L. Absorbance is dimensionless. These are simulated data for a simple teaching example; no particular reagent or actual assay is implied. Each standard is one calibration point, not a plant or a replicate treatment group.

title: Day 19 — A calibration line
text:
A laboratory instrument gives an absorbance reading, but we want a concentration. We first measure solutions of known concentration, called standards. Can a straight line describe their readings well enough to estimate the concentration of an unknown sample?
This is a common quantitative laboratory workflow. The prepared standards in data/calibration.csv cover 0–10 mg/L. Absorbance is dimensionless. These are simulated data for a simple teaching example; no particular reagent or actual assay is implied. Each standard is one calibration point, not a plant or a replicate treatment group.

title: Day 19 — A calibration line
section: Put known concentration on the horizontal axis
text:
Put known concentration on the horizontal axis

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

standards <- read_csv("data/calibration.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
calibration_plot <- ggplot(standards,
                          aes(x = concentration_mg_l, y = absorbance)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Known concentration (mg/L)", y = "Absorbance") +
  theme_minimal()
calibration_plot

The readings increase approximately along a line. We describe that line as absorbance = intercept + slope × concentration. The intercept is the fitted reading at concentration zero. The slope is the fitted increase in absorbance for a one mg/L increase in concentration. A fitted line summarises the relation; it does not have to pass through every observation.

title: Day 19 — A calibration line
text:
Fit the line in R

calibration_fit <- lm(absorbance ~ concentration_mg_l, data = standards)
coef(calibration_fit)

lm() fits a linear model. In its formula, ~ separates the response on the left from the explanatory variable on the right. data = standards says where to find the columns. coef() extracts the fitted intercept and slope. The R documentation for lm is a reference; we use only this simple straight-line case.
Your fitted coefficients should be approximately 0.03957 for the intercept and 0.06489 for the slope. Thus the line is approximately absorbance = 0.03957 + 0.06489 × concentration.

calibration_plot <- calibration_plot +
  geom_abline(intercept = coef(calibration_fit)[1],
              slope = coef(calibration_fit)[2], colour = "steelblue")
calibration_plot

The [1] and [2] select the first and second coefficients. We retain the full-precision values for calculations; rounded values are useful for prose. The nonzero intercept may represent a background reading. Do not force the line through zero merely because concentration zero sounds like “nothing”.



Prepared standards and their fitted calibration line.

title: Day 19 — A calibration line
text:
Check deviations from the line
A residual is an observed reading minus the line’s fitted reading. Positive means the point is above the line; negative means it is below. Residuals have absorbance units here.

standards <- standards |>
  mutate(fitted_absorbance = fitted(calibration_fit),
         residual = residuals(calibration_fit))
standards

residual_plot <- ggplot(standards,
                        aes(x = concentration_mg_l, y = residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Known concentration (mg/L)", y = "Residual absorbance") +
  theme_minimal()
residual_plot




Deviations of standard readings from the fitted line, in absorbance units.


Look for curvature or a point that stands apart, not for all residuals to be positive or negative. These six small residuals show no obvious curved pattern. Six standards are still limited evidence: the picture does not guarantee that the relationship holds at arbitrary concentrations.

title: Day 19 — A calibration line
section: Estimate the unknowns within the calibration range
text:
Estimate the unknowns within the calibration range
Rearranging the line gives concentration = (absorbance − intercept) / slope. This is a point estimate; we are not calculating a full uncertainty interval for the unknown concentration.

unknowns <- read_csv("data/unknowns.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
intercept <- coef(calibration_fit)[1]
slope <- coef(calibration_fit)[2]

unknowns <- unknowns |>
  mutate(within_range = absorbance >= min(standards$absorbance) &
                        absorbance <= max(standards$absorbance),
         concentration_mg_l = if_else(
           within_range, (absorbance - intercept) / slope, NA_real_))
unknowns

The & requires both range conditions. if_else() assigns a numeric missing value, NA_real_, to unsupported estimates. U1 is about 4.17 mg/L and U2 about 7.40 mg/L. U3 exceeds the largest measured standard reading. Report it as outside the calibration range; do not present an extrapolated value as a valid result. A real laboratory might dilute the sample and measure it again using its assay protocol. Do not invent a dilution correction without such a measurement.

title: Day 19 — A calibration line
section: Transfer question: a newly measured dilution
text:
Transfer question: a newly measured dilution
Use this short calculation as a transfer check, rather than doing another complete calibration exercise. A dilution mixes some original solution with solvent to reach a larger final total volume. Assume that no measured substance is lost or reacts. Its concentration is reduced by the factor final total volume / original-sample volume.
A separate unknown was outside the instrument range. A new measurement is now provided: 1.00 mL of the original was diluted to a total of 10.00 mL, and the diluted reading was 0.520. This is not an instruction to add 10 mL of solvent, and it is not a new reading for U3. All data remain simulated.

Check that 0.520 is inside the measured standard-reading range.
Use the fitted line to calculate the diluted concentration in mg/L.
Multiply by 10.00 / 1.00 to estimate the original concentration.
State why this differs from extrapolating a line beyond its measured range.







Hint and numerical check





diluted_absorbance <- 0.520
dilution_factor <- 10.00 / 1.00
diluted_mg_l <- (diluted_absorbance - intercept) / slope
original_mg_l <- diluted_mg_l * dilution_factor
c(diluted_mg_l = diluted_mg_l, original_mg_l = original_mg_l)
Using unrounded coefficients, the estimates are about 7.40 mg/L diluted and 74.04 mg/L original. The diluted reading is within range; the original estimate follows from that new reading and a stated dilution factor. This does not make U3’s old out-of-range reading valid. Full measurement, dilution, and calibration uncertainty are still omitted from these point estimates.

title: Day 19 — A calibration line
text:
Practical and saved work
Create calibration-report.Rmd at the project root. Explain what a standard is, include the line and residual plots, describe the slope with units, and report the two supported concentration estimates. Explain why U3 needs another step. State that these simple inverse estimates omit full calibration uncertainty. Save the table with write_csv(unknowns, "output/day19-unknowns.csv") and both figures with ggsave(). Render after restarting R.






Hint: which way round is the model?





We prepared concentration and measured absorbance, so we fit absorbance as the response. We then rearrange that fitted line. Fitting concentration as a response is a different regression and is not the workflow used here.

title: Day 19 — A calibration line
text:
Check your understanding

What does a positive residual mean? The observed reading is above the line.
Does a good fit from 0–10 mg/L justify a prediction at 100 mg/L? No.
Are concentration estimates exact? No; standards, measurement, and the fitted relationship all contribute uncertainty.

Leave with: the calibration report, supported concentration table, and figures.

title: Day 17 — A guided Welch t-test
text:
Our sample shows about 6.22 mm more growth in the treated group. How uncertain is that estimated difference, and how does the experiment compare with an equal-means model? We will add a Welch two-sample t-test to yesterday’s report. We use this method for two independent groups and do not require their variances to be equal.

title: Day 17 — A guided Welch t-test
section: Check the design before calling a function
text:
Check the design before calling a function
Each value in treated is one plant’s growth; each value in control is another plant’s growth. The groups are independent, treatments were randomly assigned, and we have not selected plants according to whether their growth supports our expectations. Inspect yesterday’s plot for severe skew, questionable values, or one observation dominating a group. With small groups, these features can make the usual interval and test unreliable. Seek advice when the method looks unsuitable; do not delete valid extreme observations to improve a p-value.
The test does not repair dependence, biased sampling, or measurement errors. We are using a small, deliberately simple dataset to learn an analysis workflow.

title: Day 17 — A guided Welch t-test
section: Run the comparison in the direction we stated
text:
Run the comparison in the direction we stated

comparison <- t.test(treated, control, var.equal = FALSE,
                     alternative = "two.sided", conf.level = 0.95)
comparison

The first vector is treated, the second control. The confidence interval therefore describes treated minus control. var.equal = FALSE explicitly selects Welch’s method. The other arguments make our two-sided question and interval level visible. You can inspect arguments with ?t.test; the R documentation also describes the returned result.
For these simulated data, key parts of the output are approximately:
Welch Two Sample t-test
p-value = 0.001517
95 percent confidence interval:
 2.701  9.732
sample estimates:
mean of x  mean of y
 21.4917    15.2750
Small printing differences are normal. The t statistic and degrees of freedom are part of the calculation; you do not need to derive them here. Concentrate on the question, difference, interval, and assumptions.

title: Day 17 — A guided Welch t-test
section: Read the result in a useful order
text:
Read the result in a useful order
First state the estimated effect: treated plants grew on average 6.22 mm more than controls in our sample. Then state its 95% confidence interval: about 2.70 to 9.73 mm for the population mean difference, under the model assumptions.
The interval expresses uncertainty in a mean difference. It is not a range containing 95% of individual plants. A 95% confidence procedure would cover the true difference in about 95% of repeated experiments under its assumptions. This particular interval either covers that fixed difference or does not; we do not know which. Values near the interval’s centre fit the data better than more distant values, rather than all values in the interval being equally plausible.
Finally report the p-value, about 0.0015. An equal-means model would rarely produce a two-sided t statistic at least this extreme under the assumptions. This is evidence against equal population means in this model. It is not a 99.85% probability that the treatment works, and it does not tell us whether 6 mm matters biologically. That judgment needs the organism, duration, and purpose of the study.

title: Day 17 — A guided Welch t-test
text:
Practical: extend your report
Add a Methods paragraph naming the two independent groups, growth calculation, direction of comparison, and Welch two-sample t-test. Keep the individual-point plot. Add the test chunk and a Results paragraph with the two means, sample sizes, estimated difference, interval, and p-value. A possible structure is:

In these simulated observations, mean growth was … in … and … in … . The estimated treated-minus-control difference was … mm (95% confidence interval … to … mm; Welch two-sample t-test, p = …). This suggests … under … .

Use your own words for the last sentence. Do not report only “significant”.
Extract numbers rather than retyping a long printout:

mean(treated) - mean(control)
comparison$conf.int
comparison$p.value

The $ selects a named component of the result. The interval’s two endpoints are the lower and upper limits in the direction we selected. If you later use a formula interface, check its group order carefully; the sign may reverse.






Hint: what if the interval includes zero?





Zero represents equal population means for this comparison. An interval spanning zero would show that the data do not resolve the direction at this confidence level. It would not establish equivalence or prove that there is no effect.

title: Day 17 — A guided Welch t-test
text:
Check your understanding

Which has units of millimetres: the difference, the interval, or the p-value? The first two; a p-value has no measurement units.
Does group SD describe uncertainty in the difference? No; SD describes individual spread within a group.
If all these plants came from one shared pot per treatment, would the same analysis be justified? No; the independent-unit assumption would change.

title: Day 15 — Describe the experiment without overstating it
section: Build the report in a clear order
text:
Build the report in a clear order
Use this order inside the report:

Load packages and import the input file.
Inspect its structure and document relevant data checks.
Derive growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm.
Calculate the grouped summary with sample counts, mean, median, and SD.
Draw the individual-plant figure with group means.
Explain the centre, spread, overlap, and limitations in ordinary language.

Here is a compact data-check block that can appear after import:

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
anyDuplicated(seedlings$plant_id)
seedlings |> count(treatment)
sum(is.na(seedlings$initial_mm))
sum(is.na(seedlings$final_mm))
seedlings <- mutate(seedlings, growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)

anyDuplicated() returns zero when it finds no duplicate; a positive result identifies the position of the first duplicate, not a count of duplicates. Include only checking output that helps the reader, but keep the code available in the source. Reuse your day 13 summary and figure rather than replacing them with a screenshot of the RStudio Environment pane.
A table in an R Markdown chunk can be displayed neatly with:

group_summary <- seedlings |>
  group_by(treatment) |>
  summarise(n_observed = sum(!is.na(growth_mm)),
            mean_mm = mean(growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            median_mm = median(growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd_mm = sd(growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
knitr::kable(group_summary, digits = 2,
             caption = "Observed growth and variation by treatment; lengths in mm.")

The table is generated from code. If the data change, the rendered table can change too. A caption must distinguish SD among plants from uncertainty in the mean. This report has SD, not confidence intervals.

title: Day 15 — Describe the experiment without overstating it
section: Write with the question in view
text:
Write with the question in view
A useful description distinguishes three ideas: group averages differ in this sample; plants vary within each group; and sample descriptions do not quantify all uncertainty about a treatment effect. You can report observed values with units and identify the independent unit without declaring a universal result.
For the complete data, the group means are about 15.3 mm for controls and 21.5 mm for treated plants. Check your table rather than copying these numbers into prose without verification. The treated group also has more spread in these data. Do not say that every treated plant outgrew every control plant: the individual observations overlap.

title: Day 15 — Describe the experiment without overstating it
text:
Alternative context: report collected-product yield
Use this in place of the seedling report if selected. The question is: what percentage of the supplied maximum product mass was collected in each run, and how does it vary between protocols? All data are simulated. A synthesis run is one independently carried-out product-making experiment. Twelve independent runs were randomly assigned to two protocols, six to each. A protocol is a specified method; no knowledge of its chemical steps is required here.
theoretical_mass_g is the supplied maximum possible product mass for that run’s starting amounts. isolated_mass_g is the dry collected product mass, assumed pure for this simplified calculation. Both are in grams. Calculate percentage yield with 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g, so Y01 is 100 * 0.62 / 1.00 = 62%. Theoretical masses differ with starting scale; compare the percentages, not the raw masses. You do not need to balance a reaction or calculate a theoretical mass yourself.

organic <- read_csv("data/organic-recovery.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(yield_percent = 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g)
organic_summary <- organic |>
  group_by(protocol) |>
  summarise(n_runs = n(), mean_yield_percent = mean(yield_percent),
            sd_percentage_points = sd(yield_percent), .groups = "drop")
organic_summary

Follow the same report order: import and check IDs, labels, numeric masses, missing values, and positive theoretical masses; calculate yield; show a table and individual-run plot; then interpret centre, spread, and overlap. Both groups have six available runs. Mean yields are about 68.67% and 77.00%; SDs are about 4.32 and 3.74 percentage points for standard and modified protocols. Label the y-axis “Isolated product yield (%)” and identify one point as one run. Do not call repeated weighings of one product batch independent runs.
This is descriptive work: no t-test is needed. A higher mean yield does not establish greater purity, safety, environmental benefit, or superiority in other reactions. Write a limitation tied to the small simulated set and the assumed purity. Keep the source and data together so the report can render from scratch.

A good limitation is specific





“The sample is small” is less informative than naming the independent unit, noting overlap or variation, and explaining that today’s report describes the sample without yet estimating uncertainty in a treatment difference. Missing observations, when present, should also be counted and discussed.

text:
How can a figure and a small table show both the typical growth and differences among individual plants? A pair of bars showing only means would conceal sample size, spread, unusual observations, and overlap. We will show the observations and use summary numbers as an additional description.
Start day13-groups.R at the project root:

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)

title: Day 13 — Summarise groups without hiding the plants
section: One row per group in a summary
text:
One row per group in a summary

group_summary <- seedlings |>
  group_by(treatment) |>
  summarise(n_plants = n(),
            n_observed = sum(!is.na(growth_mm)),
            mean_mm = mean(growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            median_mm = median(growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd_mm = sd(growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop")
group_summary

group_by(treatment) tells the next operation to work separately within each treatment. summarise() returns one row of results per group. The names on the left of = become output column names. n() counts rows; sum(!is.na(...)) counts observed measurements. Here ! means “not”, so the expression identifies values that are not missing. .groups = "drop" makes the resulting summary an ordinary ungrouped table.
This clean dataset has twelve observed growth values per group. The means are about 15.3 and 21.5 mm, and SDs about 3.19 and 4.87 mm for control and treated plants, respectively. The table is a different object from seedlings: group_summary contains two rows describing groups, not two newly measured plants.

title: Day 13 — Summarise groups without hiding the plants
text:
Add a clearly identified mean

group_plot <- ggplot(seedlings, aes(x = treatment, y = growth_mm)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0, seed = 13),
             alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_point(data = group_summary, aes(x = treatment, y = mean_mm),
             inherit.aes = FALSE, shape = 18, size = 4, colour = "darkred") +
  labs(x = "Treatment", y = "Change in seedling length (mm)",
       caption = "Small dots: individual plants. Red diamonds: group means.") +
  theme_minimal()
group_plot

The second point layer uses the summary table. Its inherit.aes = FALSE means we supply its mappings explicitly instead of inheriting a column absent from that table. You can reuse this worked pattern; understanding the two tables matters more than memorising the option today.
If adding error bars, name exactly what they represent. Mean ± SD describes spread among observations. A confidence interval describes uncertainty in an estimated mean; the two are not interchangeable. It is fine to keep today’s figure as observations and means only.

title: Day 13 — Summarise groups without hiding the plants
section: A histogram answers a different question
text:
A histogram answers a different question

ggplot(seedlings, aes(x = growth_mm)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 4, boundary = 0, colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ treatment, ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = "Change in seedling length (mm)", y = "Number of plants") +
  theme_minimal()

A histogram groups nearby numeric measurements into intervals, or bins. It shows a rough distribution, not the order in which plants were measured. With only twelve observations per group, its shape changes noticeably with the bin width. facet_wrap() gives a separate panel per treatment. Shared scales help compare the panels; small samples warrant cautious descriptions.

text:
Your practical

Reproduce the summary table and dot plot. Check one group mean using filter() and mean() as on day 12.

title: Day 13 — Summarise groups without hiding the plants
text:
Transfer choice: summarise product yield
In data/organic-recovery.csv, one row is one independently carried-out product-making experiment, or synthesis run. The supplied theoretical_mass_g is its maximum possible product mass; isolated_mass_g is dry collected product, assumed pure for this simplified exercise. Both are in grams. Derive yield_percent = 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g; the first run is 100 * 0.62 / 1.00 = 62%. No chemical reaction calculation is required.
Import the file, derive yield, then adapt today’s grouped-summary pattern to group by protocol. Report the number of runs, mean percentage yield, and SD in percentage points. Adapt the individual-point plot to show yield by protocol. Do not plot group summaries as though they were individual runs. Save output/organic-yield-summary.csv, output/organic-yield-summary.png, and its caption instead of the extra cleaned-seedling summary.






Hint: keep the denominator and the experimental unit





Use mutate(yield_percent = 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g), then group_by(protocol) and summarise(). Both groups have six independent runs. The standard mean is about 68.67% and the modified mean is 77.00%; show the individual values before interpreting the difference. Different starting scales mean that comparing raw grams would answer a different question.









Hint: keep object roles clear





write_csv(group_summary, "output/growth-summary.csv") saves the summary, while ggsave("output/growth-summary.png", plot = group_plot, width = 6, height = 4) saves the plot. These outputs have different purposes. Check names() if a layer mentions a column absent from the table used by that layer.

title: Day 13 — Summarise groups without hiding the plants
text:
Check your understanding






Why show individual dots?





Dots reveal how many observations overlap, where unusual values lie, and how measurements vary around each mean. A higher mean does not mean every treated plant grew more than every control plant. The repaired dataset retains twelve control plants but only eleven observed control growth values.



Keep: day13-groups.R, the summary CSV, figure, and caption. Next: replicates and uncertainty.

title: Day 11 — Check the table before trusting the answer
text:
What if a length was entered in the wrong unit, a plant appears twice, or a measurement is missing? R can calculate a precise-looking answer from a poor table. Our job is to check what the values mean and leave a record of justified repairs. Never edit the supplied raw file to make a calculation look convenient.
Today’s data/seedlings-messy.csv contains deliberately planted errors. Read data/field-notes.txt, which provides the source-record information needed to resolve them. This is a teaching exercise in verification, not a rule that unusual observations must be wrong.

title: Day 11 — Check the table before trusting the answer
text:
Inspect before converting
Create day11-cleaning.R in the project root. Read every column as text so that mixed entries remain visible. Keep leading/trailing spaces for this inspection.

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
raw <- read_csv("data/seedlings-messy.csv", show_col_types = FALSE,
                col_types = cols(.default = col_character()), trim_ws = FALSE)
dim(raw)
unique(raw$treatment)
filter(raw, plant_id %in% c("P01", "P06", "P18", "P21"))

cols(.default = col_character()) requests text columns instead of guessing. unique() shows distinct values, so "control" and "Control" can be noticed. %in% asks whether a value belongs to the listed set of IDs. A CSV importer may normally trim surrounding spaces; we temporarily keep them so we can see the problem rather than mistake automatic tidying for a clean source.
The file has 25 rows although the study has 24 plants. Confirm the duplicated ID:

raw |> count(plant_id) |> filter(n > 1)

count() counts rows by the named column. Repeated IDs can be legitimate if a table has one row per time point. Here the protocol says one row per plant, so we inspect both P01 rows and the source record before deciding what to do.

title: Day 11 — Check the table before trusting the answer
text:
Make evidence-based repairs
The supplied field notes establish the following:

The two P01 rows are an accidental duplicate of the same record.
Control means control, and a trailing space on a treatment is accidental.
P18’s initial length is 18.7 mm; its cell includes the unit as text.
P21’s source record gives final length 43.8 mm, not the entered 4.38.
P06’s final measurement is unavailable. There is no supported replacement.

The number 4.38 alone would not justify multiplying by ten. The source record authorises that correction. Similarly, missing P06 is not a length of zero.

cleaned <- raw |>
  mutate(treatment = tolower(trimws(treatment)),
         initial_mm = if_else(plant_id == "P18", "18.7", initial_mm),
         final_mm = if_else(plant_id == "P21", "43.8", final_mm)) |>
  distinct() |>
  mutate(initial_mm = parse_double(initial_mm),
         final_mm = parse_double(final_mm),
         growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)

trimws() removes surrounding whitespace, and tolower() standardises letters in these documented labels. if_else(condition, yes, no) makes the stated replacement only for the identified record. distinct() removes exact repeated rows; we use it only after confirming the import duplication. parse_double() turns verified number text into numeric values, preserving missing values. These are worked repair instructions, not functions to memorise today.

title: Day 11 — Check the table before trusting the answer
text:
Check the repaired table

nrow(cleaned)
anyDuplicated(cleaned$plant_id)
sum(is.na(cleaned$growth_mm))
cleaned |> count(treatment)
write_csv(cleaned, "output/seedlings-cleaned.csv")

Expect 24 rows, zero duplicated IDs, and one missing growth value. Both groups still contain 12 plants, but the control group has only 11 observed growth values. Counting enrolled plants and counting usable measurements answer different questions. Keep the raw file, repair script, and field notes so another person can trace these decisions.

title: Day 11 — Check the table before trusting the answer
text:
Your practical

Run the inspection steps before the repair block. Write comments recording what prompted each check.
Run the repairs and verify the expected counts. Inspect P06, P18, and P21.
Calculate the mean of cleaned$growth_mm with and without na.rm = TRUE. Explain what each result means; do not replace the missing value.
Save a short output/cleaning-notes.txt explaining the evidence for each change and the observation left unavailable.

Hint: avoid silently losing records





Inspect raw |> filter(plant_id == "P01") before using distinct(). Do not use distinct(plant_id, .keep_all = TRUE) to discard different records merely because they share an ID. Real disagreements need investigation.

title: Day 11 — Check the table before trusting the answer
text:
Check your understanding






What makes a repair justified?





A check identifies a question; the source record supports the repair. A very small or large value may be real. Omitting missing values from a calculation does not make their absence disappear from the report.

title: Day 9 — Make a report that runs its own calculations
text:
Open the supplied template
Open the project and then report.Rmd from its root folder. First save an unchanged backup if you want one. Keep your working .Rmd at the project root so that data/seedlings.csv points to the supplied data. Moving it into reports/ would change the relative location of the data during an ordinary knit.
The template has a short header between --- lines, including a title and output: html_document. That header configures the document. Leave the output format unchanged for now. A heading in ordinary text starts with #, while a code comment starting with # lives inside a code chunk. Their location matters.
Here is a minimal complete report. The three-backtick fences in the box belong in your .Rmd file.
---
title: "Seedling growth"
output: html_document
---

## Question

How much did the seedlings grow during the observation period?

```{r import}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
seedlings <- mutate(seedlings, growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
```

There are `r nrow(seedlings)` plants in the dataset.

```{r mean-growth}
mean(seedlings$growth_mm)
```

Growth is final minus initial length, measured in millimetres.

The fences mark where an R chunk starts and ends. Chunk labels such as import are names for sections of code and must be unique within a report. The inline expression in the sentence inserts a calculated result into prose; R executes it during rendering. You can begin with ordinary prose and add inline calculations later.

title: Day 9 — Make a report that runs its own calculations
section: Render, rather than assembling results by hand
text:
Render, rather than assembling results by hand
Save the source, then choose Knit. Rendering runs the chunks in document order and creates an HTML file. For an explicit equivalent command from the R Console, use the following command. Do not put it inside report.Rmd: a report must not try to render itself.

rmarkdown::render("report.Rmd", output_dir = "reports")

rmarkdown::render calls a function in the rmarkdown package without loading all of that package’s functions. Its output_dir puts the rendered result in reports/; the .Rmd stays at the project root. The Knit button may initially put its HTML next to the source instead. Both are HTML reports; locate the actual file rather than assuming it appeared in a particular folder.
A report must contain its imports and calculations. An object you created only in the Console may let a chunk run interactively, yet be absent during knitting. The saved source must be sufficient to rebuild the result from the saved data.

title: Day 9 — Make a report that runs its own calculations
section: Add a figure and its meaning
text:
Add a figure and its meaning
In your report, load ggplot2 and reuse the growth plot from day 8. Give the figure a caption by starting its chunk with this line:
```{r growth-figure, fig.cap="Each point represents one independently potted seedling."}
# Put the plotting code here.
```

Replace the comment with the plotting code, keeping both chunk fences. Write a sentence below the figure explaining what the vertical axis measures. A caption identifies what a figure shows; the surrounding text explains why it matters. Code can be visible in this first report so that your method is easy to inspect.

title: Day 9 — Make a report that runs its own calculations
text:
Your practical

Render the supplied template before changing it. Confirm the HTML opens.
Change its title, question, and author information; save and render again.
Put the import, growth calculation, and labelled plot in chunks in the right order. Remove repeated chunks that create the same object unnecessarily.
Add methods explaining what one row represents and how growth was calculated.
Deliberately misspell a column name, render, and read the error’s chunk name. Fix the spelling and render successfully. Practise recovery, not memorisation.
Restart R and render the document again using the command above.







Hint: rendering stops





Read the first useful error and its chunk label. Check that the document loads packages before using their functions, imports the data before calculating, and uses the exact filename and column names. Which files do you keep?

title: Day 7 — Read a table and find out what it means
text:
Start from a known place
Create day07.R in the project root. Run:

getwd()
file.exists("data/seedlings.csv")

getwd() reports R’s working directory. It should be your extracted project folder, not the data folder. The second line should return TRUE. The relative path data/seedlings.csv means “inside data, find seedlings.csv, starting here”. Your full home-folder path differs from a classmate’s; this relative path can stay the same when they open their own project.
If file.exists() returns FALSE, inspect the folder in the file manager. A common problem is opening the ZIP rather than an extracted project, or an extra folder layer. Avoid solving this by inserting your personal absolute path into every line of code. Open the correct project instead.

title: Day 7 — Read a table and find out what it means
text:
Import and inspect
The readr package provides a table importer. Packages add functions to R; installing a package puts it on disk, while library() loads it for this session. The software setup page explains installation. Loading is needed again after restarting R.

library(readr)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
head(seedlings)
dim(seedlings)
names(seedlings)
str(seedlings)

read_csv() returns a table, displayed as a tibble. head() shows its first rows, not the complete dataset. dim() gives 24 rows and 4 columns. names() returns column names. str() describes structure and types: plant_id and treatment are text; the two lengths are numeric. Suppressing the type message with show_col_types = FALSE does not remove the need to check types.
Read the first row aloud: plant P01 is in the control group; its initial length was 25.7 mm and its final length 44.3 mm. Each row represents one plant, each column one variable. Two lengths from the same row are measurements on the same plant, not two independent plants.

seedlings$initial_mm
length(seedlings$initial_mm)
mean(seedlings$initial_mm)

$ selects a named column from the table, giving a vector. The length is 24. A mean without a unit is incomplete: the average initial length is measured in mm. The numbers cannot tell you whether the file used mm or cm; the dictionary and measurement protocol provide that information.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 7 — Read a table and find out what it means
text:
Missing is different from zero
A missing measurement is represented by NA after import. NA means not available. It does not mean zero length, no growth, or a control treatment.

example_mm <- c(12, NA, 18)
mean(example_mm)
mean(example_mm, na.rm = TRUE)
is.na(example_mm)

The first mean is NA: R will not silently pretend all measurements are known. The second is 15 mm, calculated from two observed values. na.rm = TRUE requests omitting missing values for this calculation. A report must still explain how many observations were missing and why, if known.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

Run library(readr) before read_csv(). If loading fails because the package is not installed, use the setup instructions or ask for help. For column names, copy from names(seedlings); initial_mm and initial are different names.

title: Day 5 — Share laboratory files, then meet R
text:
Practical 1: a fresh investigation folder
Return to your shell workspace:
cd ~/introcomputing-shell
pwd
Use commands from the previous lessons to do the following. Read the whole list once before starting.

Create a fresh folder called day5.
Copy lab-data.zip into it and move into day5.
List the archive’s contents without extracting it.
Extract it into a folder called lab-data inside day5.
Enter the extracted folder and read the README.
Print the treated sample records and save them as treated-samples.txt.
Count the matching records using a pipe. Explain why the result is two.







Help me get started without doing everything





From the workspace use mkdir day5, cp lab-data.zip day5/, then cd day5. The slash after day5/ makes it clear that this destination is a directory. Use unzip -l lab-data.zip before unzip lab-data.zip -d lab-data. If a name already exists, inspect it before choosing whether to reuse it.









I cannot remember the search commands





Inside the extracted folder use grep -F treated samples.tsv. Add > treated-samples.txt to save the output, or | wc -l to count it. Do not redirect output into samples.tsv: that is the original input.

title: Day 5 — Share laboratory files, then meet R
section: Practical 2: make a package another person can inspect
text:
Practical 2: make a package another person can inspect
Inside the extracted lab-data folder, make a folder called report. Copy treated-samples.txt into it. Copy README.txt into it with the destination name context.txt. These copies keep the original files available.
Through the file manager, add report/findings.txt with four short statements: the number of samples, which received treatment, what the measurements mean, and what you have not yet analysed. For example, identifying a treated sample does not establish that its treatment changed growth.






Copy and rename commands





mkdir report
cp treated-samples.txt report/
cp README.txt report/context.txt
Create your own findings text in a plain-text editor. Check its saved location with ls report before packaging the folder.



Create and inspect a ZIP package:
zip -r report-bundle.zip report/
unzip -l report-bundle.zip
unzip report-bundle.zip -d review
ls review/report
zip creates an archive. -r includes the folder’s contents recursively, including any nested folders. unzip -l lets you inspect the package, then extraction into review tests what a recipient would receive. You should find context.txt, findings.txt, and treated-samples.txt inside review/report. Open findings.txt from there and check it is readable.
An archive is a snapshot of the files included when it was created or updated. Editing the ordinary report/findings.txt does not automatically update the ZIP. Make a new clearly named package after making changes. An archive stored only next to its originals is still vulnerable if the whole computer is lost.

title: Day 5 — Share laboratory files, then meet R
text:
Practical 3: choose one transfer check
Choose the partner explanation below or the organic-laboratory file task that follows. They practise the same file skills; you do not need to do both.

Explain the seedling files to a partner
Take turns. Point to the original archive, extracted source files, selected records, your findings, and the final report archive. Explain the role of each. Ask your partner to locate a particular measurement file using the manifest. Check the path rather than relying on a file that happened to be open already.
If the supported remote environment is ready, repeat just the navigation and inspection part there. Use the provided transfer route to move a small file, then identify the local and remote copies. If it is not ready, this step waits; the local practical still stands on its own.


Or: find records in a small organic-laboratory inventory
An inventory is a list of samples. Our simulated organic-chemistry inventory already labels each sample with a class, such as alcohol or ester. These are supplied text labels; you do not need to recognise a molecular structure or know its reactions. The task is simply to find the records labelled ester.

Download organic-lab.zip and locate it in your file manager. As on day 4, open ~/introcomputing-shell graphically and copy the download there. A browser download is not automatically in Ubuntu.
Return to that workspace in the shell, list the archive before extracting, then extract to a fresh organic-lab folder and enter it. Read README.txt and DICTIONARY.txt with less before inspecting inventory.tsv.
Use grep -F ester inventory.tsv to print matching records. Save them in ester-samples.txt and use a pipe to count them. Locate the saved extract in the file manager, then explain which file remained unchanged.







Hint: the same commands, different filenames





cd ~/introcomputing-shell
unzip -l organic-lab.zip
unzip organic-lab.zip -d organic-lab
cd organic-lab
less README.txt
less DICTIONARY.txt
head inventory.tsv
grep -F ester inventory.tsv > ester-samples.txt
grep -F ester inventory.tsv | wc -l
There are four sample records plus a header. Two records match: O02 and O03. The header does not contain ester. This command matches literal text, not chemical structures or a particular table column. The extracted organic-recovery.csv is for later calculations; you do not need to analyse it today. If the extraction folder already exists, inspect it and use a fresh name.

title: Day 5 — Share laboratory files, then meet R
text:
Meet R and RStudio
R is a language and computing environment for working with data. RStudio is an application that provides an editor, an R console, and other tools around R. The editor holds saved instructions; the console runs them. A terminal is a shell prompt, not an R console.
Open RStudio using the R/RStudio setup instructions. If it is not installed yet, watch the demonstration and use setup support before week 2. In the R console, enter:
44.3 - 25.7
R should return 18.6: the increase in length of plant P01, in millimetres. The console might print [1] before the answer. That marks the position of the first displayed element; it is not part of the measurement.
Enter this small supplied example in the R console:
initial_mm <- c(25.7, 24.3, 18.0)
final_mm <- c(44.3, 32.3, 32.9)
plot(initial_mm, final_mm,
     xlab = "Initial length (mm)",
     ylab = "Final length (mm)")
The c(...) pieces collect three values. <- gives each collection a name. plot(...) makes a scatter plot: each point is one plant with an initial and a final length. We will learn these ideas carefully next week; today identify the axes and check that there are three points. This example includes only three plants, not the full experiment.
Do not paste cd, grep, or unzip at the R prompt. Likewise, do not paste R calculations into the Ubuntu shell and expect R to run them automatically. When a command fails, first identify which program is reading it.

title: Day 5 — Share laboratory files, then meet R
section: From a plot to a report
text:
From a plot to a report
The teacher will show a complete HTML report generated from saved measurements and an R Markdown file. Notice the biological question, code, figure with units, and a written interpretation. The goal is to make these together so that the report can be produced again when new measurements arrive. You will build your first version next week.

text:
Check your understanding






Why inspect an archive after making it?





The name of the ZIP does not guarantee what it contains. Listing and extracting it checks the folder structure and the actual saved files a recipient gets.









Where should grep run, and where should 44.3 - 25.7 run?





Use grep in the terminal’s shell. Enter the calculation in the R console. The prompt tells you which program is waiting for instructions; learn to check it before entering a command.



Save today: a tested report-bundle.zip and the ordinary report folder. Add one sentence to findings.txt explaining how the package differs from its extracted contents. The terminal gives us another way to ask the computer to work with files. It becomes useful when we repeat a task, inspect many text records, or work on a remote computer. The folders have not become a new kind of object: we are describing the same locations using words instead of clicks.
Today we will create a small shell workspace and move between its folders. Tomorrow it will hold files from a biological laboratory exercise.

title: Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders
text:
Open the right terminal
Follow the supported Windows/Mac setup page. Windows students use Ubuntu for these commands. Mac students use Terminal. If local installation is unavailable, the teacher will help arrange a supported environment. Do not spend the lesson trying to repair system settings alone.
On Windows, Ubuntu has a different home folder from Windows itself. For this week’s terminal exercises we deliberately use a separate folder in the Ubuntu home directory. Our native RStudio project will stay in the laptop Documents folder. We will practise transferring a file between these places explicitly.
A shell reads a command and starts the requested program. The terminal is the window through which we interact with the shell. You might see something like this:
anna@laptop:~$
This is a prompt. It means the shell is ready. Your prompt will differ and may end with % on a Mac. Do not type the prompt, $, or % from an example. Type the command and press Enter once to run it.

title: Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders
text:
Worked example: where am I?
Run each line separately:
pwd
ls
pwd prints the current working directory. It might print /home/anna in Ubuntu or /Users/anna on a Mac. These are examples, not text to type. ls lists the names inside the current directory. Your list need not match anyone else’s.
Now create our workspace:
cd
mkdir -p introcomputing-shell/practice
cd introcomputing-shell
pwd
ls
cd means change directory; without a destination, it takes you home. mkdir means make directory. The option -p allows it to create the parent folder too and to accept folders that already exist. The final ls should include practice. An empty folder is still a real folder.

title: Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders
section: Check it in the file manager
text:
Check it in the file manager
In Ubuntu on Windows, run:
explorer.exe .
In Mac Terminal, run:
open .
The dot means the current directory. The graphical window should show the practice folder. Leave this window open for the next exercise. On a remote Linux system these laptop-specific commands are not the remote file-transfer method; follow the supplied remote instructions instead.

title: Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders
section: Practical 1: make a map and follow it
text:
Practical 1: make a map and follow it
From introcomputing-shell, run:
cd practice
mkdir seedlings
mkdir observations
ls
cd seedlings
pwd
cd ..
pwd
.. means the parent directory. The two pwd results should end in /practice/seedlings and /practice. Compare the file manager with this tree:
introcomputing-shell/
└── practice/
    ├── seedlings/
    └── observations/
Use the graphical window to open seedlings. Does this make the terminal move there too? Run pwd to check. Each window can have its own current location. Clicking in one does not automatically change the other.

title: Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders
text:
Commands, arguments, and options
In cd seedlings, cd is the command and seedlings is its argument: the destination. In ls -l, -l is an option asking for a longer listing. You do not need to interpret every column yet; identify which column contains names.
Try these from practice:
ls -l
cd observations
ls
An empty listing from ls means there are no visible entries to list. It does not mean the command failed. Many commands report success by simply returning to the prompt.

title: Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders
section: Practical 2: recover from an ordinary mistake
text:
Practical 2: recover from an ordinary mistake
Return to practice with cd .., then try cd Observations. We created observations with a lowercase o. Ubuntu distinguishes uppercase and lowercase names. Many Macs do not distinguish them on their default disk, so this may work there. Always match the actual spelling so your work transfers between computers.
Now deliberately try:
cd no-such-folder
Read the message. The folder is missing; your computer has not broken. Run pwd and ls before trying again. Ask “where am I, and what is actually here?”






I’m lost. How can I return to the workspace?





Run cd ~/introcomputing-shell, then pwd. ~ is shorthand for your home directory. This route works even if you have navigated into several nested folders. Do not replace it with someone else’s username.

title: Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders
section: Small keyboard habits that save effort
text:
Small keyboard habits that save effort

Tab: type the first few letters of a folder, then Tab to complete a name when it is unambiguous. Try cd pra then Tab from the workspace.
Up arrow: recall a previous command. Read it before running it again.
Ctrl+C: interrupt a running command or clear a partly typed command. This is different from copying selected text. Ubuntu terminal windows commonly use Ctrl+Shift+C/V for copying and pasting; Mac uses Command+C/V.
Quotes: keep a name containing spaces together, for example mkdir "field notes". Without quotes those words can become separate arguments.

We are not using deletion commands today. Practise on the supplied workspace, and ask before removing something you did not mean to create.

title: Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders
text:
Check your understanding






What changes when I run cd? What stays unchanged?





The terminal’s current working directory changes. The files do not move, and other windows need not change location. pwd checks the new starting point.









Why can ls work without printing any filenames?





The directory may be empty. Compare with an error, which normally includes a message explaining the problem. Read the output rather than assuming silence is failure.



Save today: the shell workspace and its folder tree. In a plain-text file called navigation-notes.txt inside that workspace, record the full path printed by pwd, your route back from home, and three commands with their meanings. Create the note through the graphical window if that is easiest.
Next: open an archive of laboratory files.

title: Day 1 — Find, save, and reopen your laboratory files
text:
Did seedlings grow differently after a treatment? Before we calculate anything, we need to know which measurements belong to which plant and where those measurements are saved. A useful analysis starts with finding the right file.
Our measurements are simulated teaching data, not observations from an actual experiment. Imagine 24 seedlings, each in its own pot. Twelve pots received a treatment and twelve were controls. We measured each plant at the beginning and end. The treatment was assigned randomly. A control is a comparison group: it helps us judge what might have happened without the treatment.
Today you will download the course files, identify a table of measurements, and find your work again after closing every window. No programming is needed.

title: Day 1 — Find, save, and reopen your laboratory files
section: A file is different from the application that opens it
text:
A file is different from the application that opens it
A file is a saved collection of information with a name. A photograph, a table of measurements, and a written report can each be files. An application is a program that opens or changes files. The same table can be opened by several applications.
For example, seedlings.csv is a file. Excel, a text editor, and R can all read it. Closing Excel does not delete the saved file. Deleting the saved file is a different action. A file can also exist without any application displaying it.
A folder, also called a directory, groups files and other folders. Your computer’s file system organises these folders and records where files are stored. You can explore it using File Explorer on Windows or Finder on Mac. A browser such as Firefox or Safari displays websites; it is a different application from the file manager.

title: Day 1 — Find, save, and reopen your laboratory files
section: Practical 1: download and locate the course folder
text:
Practical 1: download and locate the course folder

Download the course files.
Open the browser’s downloads list. Use its option to show the download in File Explorer or Finder. Notice the folder’s name, usually Downloads.
Find course-files.zip. A ZIP archive is a package containing files and folders. On Windows, right-click it and choose Extract All. On Mac, double-click it to extract it. If the browser already extracted it, locate the resulting folder instead.
Find the extracted folder called introcomputing-course. Move this ordinary folder into Documents using the file manager. Do not work inside the ZIP’s preview window.
Open introcomputing-course. You should see a data folder, an output folder, a reports folder, report.Rmd, and introcomputing.Rproj.
Open data and find seedlings.csv. Keep this file unchanged.

Your computer may have a cloud-managed Documents folder. Tell the teacher if it does: we will check that your course files are actually available on the laptop, including when the network is disconnected. A shortcut or a cloud icon is not the same thing as a complete local copy.






I see two course folders. Which should I use?





Extraction can create an extra outer folder. Open folders until you find the one that directly contains data, output, and introcomputing.Rproj. That is the project folder. Move that whole folder together. Ask for help if filenames end in (1) because you downloaded several copies; choose one working copy rather than guessing between them later.

title: Day 1 — Find, save, and reopen your laboratory files
text:
Reading names and extensions
The final part of a filename, such as .csv or .jpg, is its extension. It gives a clue about the format of the saved information. A CSV is a text table in which commas separate values. Changing the name seedlings.csv to seedlings.jpg would not turn measurements into a photograph.
Make extensions visible. In Windows File Explorer, look for View → Show → File name extensions; older versions place the checkbox directly under View. In Finder, use Settings → Advanced → Show all filename extensions. Menu wording can vary. Ask for help if you cannot find the setting.

title: Day 1 — Find, save, and reopen your laboratory files
section: Practical 2: open a copy in two ways
text:
Practical 2: open a copy in two ways

Copy data/seedlings.csv and paste the copy into output.
Rename the copy seedlings-practice.csv. Confirm that it still ends in .csv.
Open this practice copy. If a spreadsheet opens automatically, notice its rows and columns, then close it without saving changes.
Right-click the practice file and choose Open with a text editor, such as Notepad on Windows or TextEdit on Mac. Do not save changes here either.

The first lines should contain the following information:
plant_id,treatment,initial_mm,final_mm
P01,control,25.7,44.3
P02,control,24.3,32.3
The first line is a header naming the columns. The next line describes plant P01. Its initial length was 25.7 millimetres and its final length was 44.3 millimetres. A spreadsheet displays the commas as column boundaries; the text editor displays the commas themselves. Both applications opened the same file.
Discuss: did P01 grow by 44.3 mm, or did it end at 44.3 mm? Its increase was 44.3 − 25.7 = 18.6 mm. Keeping the meaning and units of a measurement matters as much as knowing how to open its file.

title: Day 1 — Find, save, and reopen your laboratory files
section: Practical 3: save a note you can find again
text:
Practical 3: save a note you can find again
Open a plain-text editor and write three short sentences: what a row represents, what the length units are, and where the original measurements are stored. Use Save As and save the note as day01-notes.txt in reports.
On Mac, choose Format → Make Plain Text in TextEdit before saving. On either system, check the resulting filename in the file manager. It should not secretly end in .txt.txt or .rtf.
Close the editor and all file-manager windows. Open the file manager again and navigate from Documents to your note. Open it. If you can only find it through an application’s “recent files” list, repeat the folder route once more.

title: Day 1 — Find, save, and reopen your laboratory files
text:
Check your understanding
Try answering before opening the explanation.






Does closing an application delete the file? What did copying create?





Closing an application does not delete a saved file. Copying created another file. Changes to your practice copy would not automatically change the original. Neither copy is protected against losing the computer if both are stored only on that computer.









Why keep data/seedlings.csv unchanged?





It is our starting record. Later we will describe changes in code so that someone else can repeat the analysis and see what happened to the original measurements.



Save today: reports/day01-notes.txt and output/seedlings-practice.csv. Be ready to show their locations without relying on “recent files”.
Next: folders, paths, and what a computer does.

title: Statistics reference: describe, compare, and interpret
text:
Start with the biological question and the independent experimental unit. Neither a large table nor a small p-value can repair a design with no independent replication.
An interval around the mean does not describe where 95% of individual plants will fall. Adding technical repeats of the same plant does not add independent plants to the sample size.

title: Statistics reference: describe, compare, and interpret
text:
The two comparisons taught here
Independent groups: separate plants/pots allocated to control and treatment. Use a guided Welch two-sample t-test for the difference in mean growth. Define the direction before reporting it, such as treated minus control.
Paired observations: the same plant before and after a change. Compute after minus before within each plant, then analyse the differences. Correctly matching identifiers is essential; row order in two files is not evidence of matching pairs.
Both approaches need independent experimental units or pairs. For small samples, inspect unusual observations and strong skew. A test is conditional on its assumptions; you are not learning an automatic test-selection algorithm.
A p-value is the probability, under the null model and its assumptions, of a test statistic at least as extreme as the observed one. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true. Report the estimated difference, its units, confidence interval, sample sizes, and a biological interpretation. A small p-value does not establish a large or causal effect; a large one does not establish equality.

title: Statistics reference: describe, compare, and interpret
text:
A straight line
In lm(y ~ x, data = table), the intercept is fitted y at x = 0 and the slope is the fitted change in y for a one-unit increase in x. The slope’s units are y-units per x-unit. The residual is observed y minus fitted y.
For calibration, standards have known x values; invert the fitted line to obtain an unknown concentration from its signal, only within a supported range. This simple calculation provides a point estimate, without full uncertainty propagation. For an observational biological association, the slope does not establish what would happen if we intervened to change x.
See week 3 and week 4 for worked examples.

title: Glossary: words we use in this course
text:
Word
Meaning here




File
A named, saved collection of information, such as text, measurements, or a picture


Folder / directory
A container organising files and other folders


File system
The way an operating system stores and organises files and directories


Path
An address locating a file or directory on a particular computer


Extension
A filename ending such as .csv, .R, .Rmd, or .html, indicating its intended format


Home directory
The starting personal folder for an account on a computer


Working directory
The folder relative paths currently start from


Operating system
Software managing the computer and the applications running on it


CPU
The processor that carries out instructions


RAM / memory
Working storage used by running programs; save work to persistent files


Process
A running instance of a program


Bit / byte
A bit is 0 or 1; a byte contains eight bits, with 256 possible patterns


Terminal
A window or interface through which you interact with a shell


Shell
A program interpreting commands such as cd and ls


Console
In this course, usually the R interface that reads R expressions


Local / remote
On your current laptop / on another computer reached over a network


SSH
A secure connection to a remote shell


Remote desktop
A graphical session on a remote computer


Archive
A package containing files and folders, for example a ZIP


CSV / TSV
Text tables whose fields are separated by commas / tabs


Object
A named value held in an R session


Function
A named operation applied to inputs, such as mean()


Argument
An input or setting given to a function or command


Package
A collection of R functions and related resources


Observation
A recorded measurement or set of measurements; not necessarily an independent replicate


Experimental unit
The independently allocated entity, such as a pot or culture flask


Technical replicate
A repeated measurement of the same underlying sample


Missing value
A measurement that is unavailable; represented by NA in R


Raw data
The original supplied measurements, preserved without overwriting


Theoretical mass
In the organic practice, the supplied maximum possible product mass for a run


Isolated mass
In the organic practice, the dry product collected, assumed pure for the simplified calculation


Percentage yield
100 × isolated mass / theoretical mass, using the same mass units


Percentage point
A difference on a percentage scale: 70% minus 60% is 10 percentage points


Derived data
Values calculated or cleaned from the originals with documented code


Render / Knit
Run a report’s code and combine results with its text to create a document


Reproducibility
Being able to regenerate a result from its stated inputs, code, and environment

title: Windows: install Ubuntu; Mac: open Terminal
text:
We will use a terminal to give the computer short written instructions. On Windows we use Ubuntu, a version of Linux, through Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL). Mac users can use the Terminal application already on their Mac.
You do not need to understand the commands yet. This page gets you ready for the first exercises. Installation help will be provided during the course.
