title: Windows: install Ubuntu; Mac: open Terminal
text:
Windows: install Ubuntu

1. Prepare
Save your work: installation may require restarting your computer. You need an internet connection and permission to install software. On a university-managed computer, ask the teaching team if administrator access is unavailable.
Use Windows 11 for this setup. Microsoft’s installation command also supports Windows 10 version 2004 (build 19041) or later; if you have an older system, ask for help choosing a supported course environment.


2. Open PowerShell as administrator
Open Start, type PowerShell, right-click Windows PowerShell, and choose Run as administrator. Accept the Windows permission prompt.
PowerShell is a Windows command window. We use it for installation; later Linux exercises belong in Ubuntu.


3. Install
In PowerShell, type this command and press Enter:
wsl --install -d Ubuntu
Wait for it to finish and restart the computer if requested. This installs Ubuntu alongside your Windows applications using WSL.
These steps follow Microsoft’s WSL installation instructions.


4. Open Ubuntu and create your Linux account
After restarting, open Start, search for Ubuntu, and open it. First startup may take a little time.
When asked, choose a Linux username, for example anna, using lowercase letters. Then choose a password and enter it again when prompted. This is a separate account from your Windows account.
Nothing appears while you type the password, not even dots. This is normal. Type it and press Enter. Keep the password somewhere secure; do not send it to a teacher or include it in a screenshot.
When setup finishes, you should see a line ending in a prompt, often $. The prompt means Ubuntu is waiting for a command. Do not type the $ itself.
The account and password behaviour is described in Microsoft’s environment setup guide.


5. Check Ubuntu
In Ubuntu, run these commands one at a time:
whoami
pwd
uname -s
whoami should show your Linux username. pwd shows your current folder, usually /home/ followed by your username. uname -s should print Linux.
To check WSL itself, open PowerShell and run:
wsl --list --verbose
Look for an Ubuntu entry with 2 in the VERSION column. A running or stopped state is normal. If your installation shows version 1, bring it to the setup session so we can help check it.


6. Opening Ubuntu next time
Open Ubuntu from Start. You normally do not need administrator mode for course exercises. Closing its window does not delete your saved files.

title: Windows: install Ubuntu; Mac: open Terminal
text:
Mac: use Terminal directly
Open Finder, then Applications → Utilities → Terminal. You can also search for Terminal with Spotlight. You do not need to install Ubuntu.
Run the same three commands:
whoami
pwd
uname -s
Your home folder is usually /Users/ followed by your username, and uname -s prints Darwin, the underlying macOS system. That is expected. macOS is not Linux, but the basic commands we use work in both environments. A prompt ending in % is also normal on a Mac.
Commands labelled Ubuntu only, such as apt, do not belong in Mac Terminal.

title: Windows: install Ubuntu; Mac: open Terminal
section: First exercise: a folder you can find again
text:
First exercise: a folder you can find again
On Windows use Ubuntu; on Mac use Terminal. Run one line at a time:
cd
mkdir -p introcomputing/first-session
cd introcomputing/first-session
pwd
ls

cd on its own takes you to your home folder.
mkdir -p creates the named folders if they do not already exist.
cd introcomputing/first-session moves into that folder.
pwd prints its full location, called its path.
ls lists what is inside. A new, empty folder produces no listed filenames.

Now see the same folder in a graphical file manager:
Windows — run in Ubuntu:
explorer.exe .
Mac — run in Terminal:
open .
The dot means “the folder I am in now”. The file-manager window and the terminal are showing the same place in two different ways.
Close the terminal, reopen it, and find your folder again:
cd ~/introcomputing/first-session
pwd
Here ~ is shorthand for your home folder. Being able to return to saved work is part of being ready, even when the folder is still empty.

On Windows, Ubuntu’s /home/anna is different from Windows’ C:\Users\anna. A file downloaded by your Windows browser does not automatically appear in your Ubuntu home folder. For terminal exercises, use the Ubuntu home folder we just created. We will practise locating downloads and transferring files together.
You can reach Ubuntu files through explorer.exe ., or by entering \\wsl$ in File Explorer’s address bar and opening your Ubuntu distribution. See Microsoft’s guide to Windows and Linux file systems.

title: Install R and RStudio; open your course project
text:
R performs calculations. RStudio is the application in which we write code, inspect results, and make reports. Install both on your laptop, or use the supported remote applications when access details are provided.
These steps are for native Windows or macOS applications. Windows students do not need to install a second copy of R inside Ubuntu/WSL. The Linux command-line setup is a separate page.

title: Install R and RStudio; open your course project
text:
1. Install R
Go to CRAN’s R downloads and choose your operating system. On Windows choose the base installation, then the standard installer. On Mac choose the installer matching your Mac’s processor and supported macOS version; About This Mac identifies the processor. If the choices are unclear, bring your computer to the setup session. Install R before RStudio.
R is available for Windows, macOS, and Linux through the R Project and CRAN.

title: Install R and RStudio; open your course project
text:
2. Install RStudio Desktop
Download the free RStudio Desktop installer from Posit. Choose your operating system, install it, then open RStudio. You do not need to purchase a product or create a cloud account. Check the download page’s current system requirements if your computer is older. RStudio requires an R installation, as explained in Posit’s download guide.
Find the Console pane. Its prompt is usually >. Type:
2 + 3
Press Enter. The result should be [1] 5. The [1] labels the first element printed; it is not part of your answer or something you type.

title: Install R and RStudio; open your course project
text:
3. Install the small package set
Packages add functions to R. In the R console, run this once while connected to the internet:
install.packages(c("readr", "dplyr", "ggplot2", "rmarkdown", "knitr"))
Wait until the prompt returns. Keep installation commands out of your analysis and report: they change the computer’s setup and need not run every time. Load packages in each new analysis session using library().
If asked to compile packages from source on Windows or Mac, ask for help using the available binary packages. Installing compilers is not a course exercise.

title: Install R and RStudio; open your course project
section: 4. Download and extract the course folder
text:
4. Download and extract the course folder
If you extracted the course folder during day 1, reuse that same folder and continue with step 4 below. Do not make a second project just for this setup check.

If you do not already have it, download course-files.zip.
Find it in your browser’s downloads, then show it in the file manager.
On Windows, right-click and choose Extract All; on Mac, double-click the ZIP. Move the extracted introcomputing-course folder to a place you can find again, such as Documents. Extract the whole folder, not a single file.
Inside the extracted folder, open introcomputing.Rproj in RStudio. A ZIP preview in Windows is not an extracted project.

Your folder should look like this:
introcomputing-course/
├── introcomputing.Rproj
├── report.Rmd
├── START-HERE.txt
├── data/
│   ├── README.md
│   ├── seedlings.csv
│   └── ...
├── output/
└── reports/
The .Rproj file tells RStudio which folder is this project. Data remain ordinary files inside it. In the R console run:
getwd()
file.exists("data/seedlings.csv")
The first result should end with introcomputing-course; the second should be TRUE. data/seedlings.csv means “inside the data folder of this project”. Do not replace it with a path containing your own username.

5. Check packages and the first report
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
packageVersion("rmarkdown")
If these commands finish without an error, open report.Rmd from RStudio’s Files pane and click Knit. A report with a table and a growth plot should appear. Its data are simulated. You will learn to explain and modify this report in week 2; you are checking the installation now.
R Markdown uses Pandoc to make the output document; RStudio supplies it. You do not need a PDF/LaTeX installation for our HTML reports. R Markdown’s installation documentation describes these dependencies.

title: Data Analysis in Life Sciences
text:
Learn how computers organise information, how to work in a Linux command line, and how to use R to turn biological measurements into figures and reproducible reports.
We start with files and folders. You do not need previous programming experience. Each lesson combines an explanation, a worked example, and a practical where you save something you can find and use again. The biology includes seedling growth, photosynthesis, calibration measurements, and a small duckweed experiment. Short transfer choices also use basic organic-laboratory records, such as the percentage of a supplied maximum product mass collected. Each exercise explains the required quantities and calculation; prior chemistry is not required.

Your five-week route



Week

2 — R and reports

3 — Variation
How much do individual plants differ?
Check data, summarise groups, understand mean, variance, SD, and replication


4 — Comparisons and lines
How do treatments and measurements relate?
Interpret a t-test, handle pairs, fit a calibration line, and describe an association


5 — Reproducibility
Can someone repeat our analysis?
Work remotely, analyse another dataset, package a report, and test it in a fresh session

text:
Getting started

Windows: install Ubuntu; Mac: open Terminal.
Install R and RStudio, then open your project.
Download the course project and laboratory archive.
Working on a remote Linux computer.

Remote connection instructions will be added when the course environment is confirmed. Installation help will be provided during the course.
Begin with Day 1: save, find, and reopen a file. You can keep the terminal reference, R reference, statistics reference, and glossary open while working. Using a reference is part of the workflow, not a sign that you should have memorised everything.

title: What you will learn and how to work
text: Data Analysis in Life Sciences is a five-week introduction to computing and biological data analysis. We start with finding a file and end with an analysis that another person can reproduce. The workflow is meant to carry into later biology practicals, where R replaces manual spreadsheet calculations and graph preparation.

title: What you will learn and how to work
section: What you should become able to do
text:
What you should become able to do

Explain files, folders, paths, applications, memory, storage, and processes through the practical actions you use every day.
Organise and inspect lab files with a small set of command-line tools.
Connect to a supplied remote Linux environment and distinguish its files from the files on your laptop.
Import and check biological measurements in R, calculate derived variables, summarise groups, and make labelled plots.
Interpret mean, variance, SD, and the difference between individual spread and uncertainty in an estimate.
Interpret a guided t-test and a straight-line fit, with attention to independent experimental units, units of measurement, and limitations.
Write and render an R Markdown report from its saved data and code.

No previous file-system, terminal, R, or statistics knowledge is assumed. We will practise the same actions several times, with gradually less guidance. Later courses will develop biological theory and bioinformatics tools; this course does not teach database searching, sequence alignment, or omics analysis.
Prior chemistry courses are not required to understand an exercise. Chemistry contexts supply all definitions, inputs, constants, units, and calculation relationships. For example, percentage yield means 100 times the collected mass divided by a supplied maximum possible mass. You are practising data handling and interpretation, not deriving a chemical reaction. Where a practical offers a choice of biological or organic-laboratory data, complete one route rather than treating both as additional required reports.

title: What you will learn and how to work
section: A lesson is a study unit, not a full day of new lectures
text:
A lesson is a study unit, not a full day of new lectures
The numbered lessons suggest a five-week progression. Spend substantial time running examples, explaining results, recovering from mistakes, and returning to work after closing the applications. The exact contact timetable is arranged by the teaching team. If an installation fails, ask for support rather than spending the whole study unit trying unrelated system changes.
For most R lessons, a useful working rhythm is:

Open the course .Rproj and yesterday’s source file.
Read the biological question and identify what one row represents.
Predict a small example, run it, and explain the result.
Complete the practical, using hints and references as needed.
Save code, a plot or report, and a short interpretation.
Close/restart, reopen the work, and check that you can regenerate it.

Interface
Typical commands
What it acts on

Files and programs on your laptop

The prompt and window help identify the interface, but always ask which computer and folder you are using. A folder called data does not identify the computer that holds it.

What to keep
Preserve the raw data. Save R code or .Rmd source, not only a screenshot or printed number. Keep generated figures and HTML reports with their source and use the supported backup storage. Most daily exercises name a specific file to leave with; these are practice outputs, not a grading scheme.
The downloads page supplies datasets and a working report template. Reports are .Rmd files; the course website uses Quarto, which you do not need to author. We initially render HTML to keep the software setup small.

Start at Day 1 or return to the five-week route.

title: Remote Linux: SSH and remote desktop
text: We will also use HPC2N or another remote Linux environment. A remote computer is a computer you connect to over the network. Your laptop displays the session; the remote computer runs the programs and stores the files you save there.

title: Remote Linux: SSH and remote desktop
text:
Two ways to work remotely








Connection
What you see
What you use it for




SSH
A terminal on the remote computer
Navigate folders and run commands.


Remote desktop
A graphical workspace on the remote computer
Use a file manager and the applications provided for the course.



Both give access to a remote environment. Whether they share exactly the same files depends on how the service is configured; the course instructions will identify the folders to use.

title: Remote Linux: SSH and remote desktop
text:
What SSH means
SSH is a way to log in securely to another computer. The usual command has this shape:
ssh your-username@remote-computer-address
This is an explanation of the shape, not a working course command. We will supply the actual address and explain any additional authentication steps.
On Windows you can start SSH from Ubuntu; on Mac use Terminal. Once connected, commands such as pwd and ls act on the remote computer. Use exit to leave the SSH session and return to your local shell.
The first connection may ask you to trust the remote computer’s host key. Follow the course’s verification instructions before accepting it. Password prompts may show no characters while you type. Never share passwords or authentication codes.

title: Remote Linux: SSH and remote desktop
section: Always ask: which computer am I using?
text:
Always ask: which computer am I using?







Question
Why it matters




Is this terminal local or remote?
It determines where commands run.


Which folder am I in?
pwd gives the location on that computer.


Where did I save the data or report?
Saving remotely does not automatically create a laptop copy.


Where is RStudio running?
R needs access to files in its own environment.



A browser download on your laptop, a file in local Ubuntu, and a file on HPC2N can be three separate copies. Identical filenames do not make them the same file. Opening a remote desktop does not automatically transfer your laptop’s files.

All datasets are simulated teaching examples. Downloading a file is the start of the workflow: find it, extract it if needed, and place it where you can return to it. Read the project setup guide for step-by-step help.



Download

The shell practice archive is separate. On Windows, the Ubuntu home folder and your normal Windows Documents folder are different locations. A remote computer is another location again. Practise transferring one small file deliberately; do not assume these copies synchronise.

It supplies the maximum possible and collected product masses, with the calculation defined in each exercise. Choose a transfer option where a lesson offers it; you do not need to complete every context or have taken another chemistry course.

title: R reference: the small vocabulary we use
text: These examples assume that you opened the extracted course .Rproj file. Use RStudio’s R console for R, not a terminal waiting for shell commands. Save reusable code in an R script or your .Rmd report.

title: R reference: the small vocabulary we use
text:
Objects and functions
lengths_mm <- c(12, 15, 18)
mean(lengths_mm)
sd(lengths_mm)
length(lengths_mm)
<- assigns a value to a name. c() combines values into a vector. mean() computes an arithmetic mean, sd() a sample standard deviation, and length() the number of elements. Text needs quotes, as in "control". R is case-sensitive: Length and length are different names.

title: R reference: the small vocabulary we use
text:
Import, inspect, and calculate
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
head(seedlings)
names(seedlings)
nrow(seedlings)
glimpse(seedlings)

seedlings <- seedlings |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
|> means “take this result and pass it to the next function”. mutate() adds or changes columns. A calculation creates a derived measurement; it does not change the original CSV unless you explicitly write a file.
treated <- seedlings |>
  filter(treatment == "treated")

summary_table <- seedlings |>
  group_by(treatment) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_mm = mean(growth_mm), sd_mm = sd(growth_mm),
            .groups = "drop")
== compares values; it does not assign. filter() selects rows. group_by() tells summarise() which groups to summarise. For missing data, report both available and missing counts rather than silently dropping records.

title: R reference: the small vocabulary we use
section: A plot and an exported file
text:
A plot and an exported file
growth_plot <- ggplot(seedlings, aes(x = treatment, y = growth_mm)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0, seed = 7)) +
  labs(x = "Allocation", y = "Seven-day growth (mm)") +
  theme_minimal()
growth_plot
ggsave("output/growth.png", plot = growth_plot, width = 6, height = 4, dpi = 150)
write_csv(summary_table, "output/growth-summary.csv")
The + joins layers in a ggplot. Horizontal jitter separates overlapping points; height = 0 preserves their measured values. ggsave() needs an output folder that already exists; the course project includes one.

title: R reference: the small vocabulary we use
text:
Missing is not zero
x <- c(10, NA, 20)
is.na(x)
sum(is.na(x))
sum(!is.na(x))
mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)
NA denotes an unavailable value. na.rm = TRUE computes from available observations; it does not justify missingness or replace a report of how many were missing. The mean here is 15 from two available values.

title: R reference: the small vocabulary we use
text:
Error recovery







Message or symptom
Check




“object not found”
Spelling, case, and whether the line creating it ran


“could not find function”
Whether the right package was loaded


“cannot open file”
Project, path, filename case, and local versus remote computer


Console prompt is +
Unfinished quotes/brackets; press Esc and fix the expression


Report fails but console works
An object or package may exist only in your interactive session



Use ?mean, ?t.test, or ?lm to open R’s help for a named function. Ask for help with the exact error and the smallest relevant code, without credentials.

title: Terminal reference: find, inspect, and package files
text:
Use Ubuntu on Windows, Terminal on Mac, or the terminal provided remotely. Do not type the prompt ($ or %). Commands act on the computer to which the current shell belongs. Type pwd whenever you are unsure where you are.
Some commands overwrite existing files. Practise in the course workspace and read the destination name before pressing Enter. We do not need recursive deletion commands for the core practicals.

title: Terminal reference: find, inspect, and package files
text:
Paths and punctuation
~                        your home folder on this computer
.                        the current folder
..                       the parent folder
data/seedlings.csv       a relative path from the current folder
/home/anna/course        an example absolute path on Linux
cd .. moves one level up. A filename containing spaces needs quoting, for example less "field notes.txt". Use simple filenames with hyphens or underscores in your own work. Use Tab to complete names and the up arrow to recall a command. Ctrl+C interrupts a running command; it is not the copy shortcut.

title: Terminal reference: find, inspect, and package files
text:
A pipe connects programs
grep -F treated samples.tsv | wc -l
grep outputs matching lines. The | passes those lines to wc as input. There is no intermediate saved file. In our manifest, the answer is 2 because two records contain treated. This count is meaningful because each record is one line and the header does not contain the search term.

title: Terminal reference: find, inspect, and package files
text:
Redirection saves output
grep -F treated samples.tsv > treated-samples.txt
The > writes to a file instead of the screen and replaces existing contents at that path. >> appends, but we do not need it for this practical. The search does not parse a table or understand treatment groups: it matches text. It would also match untreated if that label occurred in the file.

title: Terminal reference: find, inspect, and package files
text:
Connect graphical and terminal views
In Ubuntu on Windows, explorer.exe . opens the current folder in File Explorer. On a Mac, open . opens it in Finder. These are local conveniences, not remote file-transfer commands. The remote desktop and file-transfer instructions will identify the supported remote route.
See week 1 for guided practice and remote access for the local/remote distinction.

title: Day 2 — Folders, paths, and the working computer

title: Day 2 — Folders, paths, and the working computer
text:
Folders form a tree
A folder can contain files and more folders. We can draw part of our project as a tree. Indentation shows what is inside what:
introcomputing-course/
├── introcomputing.Rproj
├── report.Rmd
├── data/
│   ├── README.md
│   └── seedlings.csv
├── output/
│   └── seedlings-practice.csv
└── reports/
    └── day01-notes.txt
This drawing omits other supplied datasets. data and reports are neighbours: neither is inside the other. Their parent folder is introcomputing-course. That folder is the project root because it is the starting point for this project’s organisation. It is not the root of the entire computer.
In the file manager, open reports, go up to its parent, and then enter data. Watch the address bar on Windows or the folder path in Finder. In Finder, View → Show Path Bar can make the route easier to see.

title: Day 2 — Folders, paths, and the working computer
section: A path gives the route to a file
text:
A path gives the route to a file
A path describes a location. These examples are illustrations: your username and exact Documents location will differ.
Windows: C:\Users\anna\Documents\introcomputing-course\data\seedlings.csv
Mac:     /Users/anna/Documents/introcomputing-course/data/seedlings.csv
Linux:   /home/anna/introcomputing-course/data/seedlings.csv
An absolute path starts from the file system’s root or drive and specifies the whole route. A relative path starts from an agreed current folder. From inside introcomputing-course, data/seedlings.csv means “enter data, then find seedlings.csv”. From inside reports, that same relative path would ask for a data folder inside reports, where it does not exist.
This is why we need to know our current working directory: the folder from which a program interprets relative paths. Next lesson we will ask the terminal to print it. Relative paths will let us move a whole project without changing every filename in the analysis.

title: Day 2 — Folders, paths, and the working computer
section: Practical 1: give directions through the tree
text:
Practical 1: give directions through the tree
Work in pairs. One person has the file-manager window; the other gives directions.

Start in the project root. Find the original seedling table.
Start in reports. Find the practice copy in output.
Return to the project root. Create a folder called practice.
Inside it, create field-notes and figures.
Copy yesterday’s note into field-notes and rename the copy seedling-observations.txt.
Draw the new part of the tree on paper. Swap roles and navigate from the drawing alone.

Prefer informative names with simple letters, numbers, and hyphens for this course. seedling-observations.txt is easier to interpret than new2.txt. We will learn to handle spaces too; simple names reduce avoidable typing errors.






I moved the whole project and now see two copies





First locate each copy and inspect its contents. A copy operation leaves the original in place; a move changes the location. Ask the teacher to help choose one working project before continuing. Do not delete a folder merely because its name looks similar to another.

title: Day 2 — Folders, paths, and the working computer
section: What happens when you open a file?
text:
What happens when you open a file?
Your laptop has several parts with different jobs:







Part
Job in our seedling example




Storage, such as an SSD
Holds the saved CSV and report between sessions.


Memory, or RAM
Holds information the running application is using now.


Processor, or CPU
Carries out instructions, such as calculating increases.


Operating system
Manages files, memory, devices, and running programs; Windows, macOS, and Linux are examples.


Application
Provides a particular tool, such as an editor, browser, or RStudio.



Opening a CSV lets an application read its saved contents. Editing text changes the application’s current working version. Saving writes that version to a file. An unsaved change may disappear when an application closes, even though the previously saved file remains. A process is a running instance of a program. An application installed on storage and a process using memory are related but different things.

title: Day 2 — Folders, paths, and the working computer
section: Practical 2: test the difference between editing and saving
text:
Practical 2: test the difference between editing and saving
Use practice/field-notes/seedling-observations.txt, not the original note.

Open the practice note and add “The plants were measured twice.”
Save, close, and reopen it. Confirm that the sentence remains.
Add “This line is an unsaved experiment.” Close the editor and choose to discard the change if asked. Reopen the file and inspect the result.

Some editors save automatically or restore unsaved documents. If yours restores the sentence, discuss that behaviour with a teacher rather than treating it as proof that saving never matters. The important check is what is actually in the saved file, and where the editor saved it.

title: Day 2 — Folders, paths, and the working computer
section: Where do local, cloud, and remote files live?
text:
Where do local, cloud, and remote files live?
A local file is on the computer you are using. A cloud service may keep a copy elsewhere and synchronise it with your laptop. A remote Linux computer is another computer we will log into. Its home folder is separate from yours. Opening its desktop does not automatically copy your downloads to it.
An archive in the same folder as the originals is convenient for sharing, but it is not protection against losing the whole laptop. Keep another copy using the university’s supported backup or storage service once the teaching team identifies it. Check that a copy completed and that you can retrieve it.

title: Day 2 — Folders, paths, and the working computer
text:
Check your understanding






From the project root, what is the relative path to yesterday’s note?





reports/day01-notes.txt. From inside reports, its name alone is sufficient: day01-notes.txt. The file did not move; your starting location changed.









Does more RAM automatically provide more room for saved photographs?





No. RAM supports running work; persistent storage holds saved files. They have different jobs. We will see this again when R objects disappear after restarting R but the saved data file is still present.



Save today: add reports/day02-map.txt with a simple folder tree, the path to seedlings.csv, and one sentence distinguishing RAM from storage. Keep the practice folder for later navigation exercises.

title: Day 4 — Unpack and inspect laboratory data

A lab partner has sent a small archive containing measurements and sample information. Before doing statistics, we need to establish what is in the archive and which files belong to the treated samples. We will do this with ordinary command-line utilities. The data are simulated for teaching.

title: Day 4 — Unpack and inspect laboratory data
section: Put the download in a known place
text:
Put the download in a known place

Download lab-data.zip with your browser.
Locate the downloaded file in File Explorer or Finder.
In your terminal, run cd ~/introcomputing-shell, then pwd.
Open that folder graphically using explorer.exe . in local Ubuntu on Windows or open . on Mac.
Copy the downloaded ZIP into this workspace using the file manager. Do not assume your Windows browser downloaded it into Ubuntu’s home folder.
Back in the terminal, run ls. Confirm that lab-data.zip appears.

On a remote computer, use the course’s supported transfer route when available. The browser’s local download is not automatically a remote file.

title: Day 4 — Unpack and inspect laboratory data
text:
Look before extracting
From ~/introcomputing-shell, run:
unzip -l lab-data.zip
The -l option lists archive contents without extracting them. Identify README.txt, samples.tsv, and the measurements and field-notes folders. There should be four measurement files, S01 through S04. The displayed sizes and dates are information about the archive entries; do not type them.
Now extract:
unzip lab-data.zip -d lab-data
cd lab-data
ls
less README.txt
The -d lab-data option chooses the destination folder. Extraction creates ordinary files you can open; it does not remove the ZIP. In less, use Space to move down, arrow keys to move by lines, and q to quit and return to the prompt. A short file may already fit on one screen.






Extraction asks whether to replace a file





You have probably extracted into the same destination before. Stop and inspect the destination in the file manager. For this first run, choose a fresh destination name if necessary and use that name in cd. Do not automatically agree to replace files that may contain your work.

title: Day 4 — Unpack and inspect laboratory data
section: Read a table without changing it
text:
Read a table without changing it
Run:
head -n 3 samples.tsv
wc -l samples.tsv
head -n 3 prints the first three lines. wc -l counts newline-terminated lines. The supplied manifest has a header and four sample records, so the count is 5, not four biological samples. Tabs separate the columns in this TSV (tab-separated values) file. A CSV uses commas instead.
The columns are sample_id, treatment, and file. Follow the file path for sample S03:
head measurements/S03.csv
Before interpreting a number, use the README to find out what it measures and which units were used. The filename locates measurements; it does not explain their biological meaning by itself.

title: Day 4 — Unpack and inspect laboratory data
text:
Search the manifest with grep
Run:
grep -F treated samples.tsv
grep prints lines matching a search. -F asks for a literal text match, so we do not need to learn pattern syntax. The supplied manifest should return two lines, S03 and S04, labelled treated.
This is text search, not an understanding of table columns or experiments. Searching for treated would also match untreated if that word were present. Our prepared labels are control and treated; the header does not contain the search word. Always inspect what a search actually selected.

title: Day 4 — Unpack and inspect laboratory data
section: Save a search, then count its records
text:
Save a search, then count its records
grep -F treated samples.tsv > treated-samples.txt
less treated-samples.txt
grep -F treated samples.tsv | wc -l
> redirects the output to a file instead of displaying it. It replaces the contents if that output file already exists. Never use the input filename on the right side here. treated-samples.txt is a new text extract; the original samples.tsv remains unchanged. It has no header, because the header did not match our search.
The vertical bar | is a pipe. It passes the matching lines from grep to wc -l, which counts them. The result should be 2. The pipe does not need an intermediate saved file. Count lines only when lines really represent the records you intend to count.

title: Day 4 — Unpack and inspect laboratory data
section: Practical: preserve and organise a working copy
text:
Practical: preserve and organise a working copy
Still inside lab-data, run:
mkdir working
cp samples.tsv working/samples-copy.tsv
mv working/samples-copy.tsv working/manifest-practice.tsv
ls working
cp creates a copy; mv moves or renames an entry. Here only the practice copy was renamed. Confirm that the original samples.tsv still exists. Both commands can replace existing destinations, so check names before running them.
Use the file manager to create observations.txt inside working. Record: how many sample records there are, which two received treatment, and which measurement file you would open for S04. Add the distinction between the five manifest lines and the four samples.

title: Day 4 — Unpack and inspect laboratory data
section: A first look at the remote computer
text:
A first look at the remote computer
The teacher will demonstrate SSH and remote desktop. SSH gives a terminal on another computer. A remote desktop gives a graphical workspace there. In either case, saved files can be on that other computer, even while your laptop displays the session.
When account details are available, follow the supplied instructions and try pwd and ls remotely. State aloud: “This command runs on ; this path is on .” If accounts are not ready, continue the local practical. Do not guess a login address.

title: Day 4 — Unpack and inspect laboratory data
text:
Check your understanding






Did grep change the manifest? Why does wc -l sometimes count a header?





grep reads the file; redirection saved its output separately. wc -l counts lines, not their meaning. The full manifest includes a header, while our saved matching lines do not. We must know the file’s structure to interpret the count.



Save today: treated-samples.txt, working/manifest-practice.tsv, and working/observations.txt in the extracted lab-data folder. Be able to show where the untouched archive and manifest are located.
Next: repeat the workflow and package your findings.

title: Day 6 — Let R keep track of a calculation
text:
A seedling was 20 mm long at the start of an experiment and 37 mm long at the end. How much did it grow? The answer is simple; our task is to make the computer keep a readable, repeatable record of how we obtained it. All plant measurements in this course are simulated teaching data, not results from a real experiment.
Open the extracted introcomputing-course folder and double-click introcomputing.Rproj. R is the program that calculates. RStudio is the workspace we use to write instructions, run R, inspect results, and prepare reports. Its Console accepts R instructions. An R script is a saved text file containing instructions. The terminal from week 1 accepts shell commands; do not type ls into the R Console or R expressions into the Ubuntu shell.

title: Day 6 — Let R keep track of a calculation
text:
Start with a calculation
Type the following in the R Console, pressing Enter after each line. Do not type the Console’s > prompt. The [1] in an answer labels the first printed element; it is not part of your measurement.

37 - 20
20 * 2
37 / 20

You should obtain 17, 40, and 1.85. The last value is a ratio, not a change in mm. The calculation can be correct while answering the wrong biological question.
Now choose File → New File → R Script, save it as day06.R in the project folder, and put this in the script:

# Measurements are lengths in millimetres.
initial_mm <- 20
final_mm <- 37
growth_mm <- final_mm - initial_mm
growth_mm

<- assigns the result on its right to a named object on its left. Read it as “store this value under this name”. A line beginning with # is a comment for people. R ignores the comment. To run a line from the editor, place the cursor on it and use Run. Saving a script does not run it; running a script does not save changes in the editor.
If RStudio is not ready, use the R and RStudio setup page. Keep the R reference sheet open while practising.
Object names are case-sensitive. growth_mm and Growth_mm are different names. An object in the Environment pane is in this R session’s memory. The script is a file on storage. Reopening the script does not recreate the object until you run the instructions.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 6 — Let R keep track of a calculation
section: One name can hold several values
text:
One name can hold several values
c() combines values into a vector, an ordered collection. Functions have names followed by parentheses; the values inside are their arguments.

initial_mm <- c(20, 22, 19)
final_mm <- c(37, 40, 34)
growth_mm <- final_mm - initial_mm
growth_mm
mean(growth_mm)
length(growth_mm)

The growth values are 17, 18, and 15 mm. R subtracts position by position here. mean() calculates their average, approximately 16.67 mm. length() counts values and gives 3. This only makes biological sense because both vectors list the same three plants in the same order. Matching observations matters.
Numbers, text, and logical values are different kinds of data:

plant_id <- c("P01", "P02", "P03")
growth_mm > 16

The comparison gives TRUE TRUE FALSE. Quotation marks identify text; "20" is text whereas 20 is a number. Plant IDs belong in text even if they contain numbers. To open help for a function, run ?mean in the Console and read its Description and Examples rather than every option.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 6 — Let R keep track of a calculation
text:
Your practical

Keep the three-plant calculation in day06.R and explain the units in comments.
Add a fourth plant that grew from 21 to 39 mm. Extend both vectors, rerun the calculation, and check length(growth_mm).
Choose one ratio exercise: calculate each plant’s final/initial ratio in an object called length_ratio, explaining how it differs from growth in mm; or use the product-yield calculation below. Both practise division and named inputs; you do not need to do both.
Change the first final length from 37 to 38 mm. Predict which growth value changes and check your prediction.
Save the script, restart R through Session → Restart R, and run its lines from the top. Everything it needs should be in the script.


Alternative ratio exercise: how much product was collected?
In a synthesis, starting materials are used to make a product. For this simulated example, the maximum possible product mass has already been calculated for you: 1.00 g. Call it theoretical_mass_g. The collected dry product has mass 0.62 g, called isolated_mass_g. Assume this collected material is pure product for this simplified calculation. You do not need a reaction equation.
Percentage yield means the collected product as a percentage of the supplied maximum. Compute 100 × isolated mass / theoretical mass, using the same mass unit for both. Put this calculation in day06.R if you chose this alternative:

theoretical_mass_g <- 1.00
isolated_mass_g <- 0.62
yield_percent <- 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g
yield_percent

The answer is 62%. The gram units cancel in the ratio. Predict the result if collected mass changes to 0.70 g, then rerun; it should be 70%. Add a comment explaining why 0.62 g is a mass and 62% is a proportion relative to a maximum. A larger percentage does not establish greater purity or safety. This is numerical practice, not instructions for carrying out a chemical experiment.






Hint: an object is not found





Check the spelling, including capitals, and run the line that creates the object. An editor line has no effect until it runs. If the Console shows +, an expression is unfinished: check quotes or parentheses, or press Esc to cancel it.

title: Day 6 — Let R keep track of a calculation
text:
Check your understanding

What survives restarting R: an unsaved object or a saved script?
Why is mean(plant_id) not a useful operation?
What must be true for two vectors to be subtracted position by position?







Check your answers





The saved script survives; objects must be recreated. IDs name plants rather than measure quantities, so an average ID has no meaning. The vectors must refer to corresponding observations in the same order and have compatible lengths.



Keep: day06.R, with the four-plant example and comments about units. Next: import a whole table.

title: Day 8 — Turn measurements into a useful figure
text: Do plants that started longer also end longer? And how much did each plant grow? A new column and a labelled figure can answer these questions without editing cells by hand. Start a script called day08.R in your project root.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 8 — Turn measurements into a useful figure
text:
Create a derived measurement

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
seedlings <- mutate(seedlings, growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
head(seedlings)

mutate() returns a table with a new or changed column. We assign that returned table to seedlings. Within this function, R looks for final_mm and initial_mm in the supplied table. The original file on disk is unchanged. For P01, check 44.3 minus 25.7: the growth is 18.6 mm. A negative change would mean the recorded final length was smaller; it would deserve checking, not automatic deletion.
The new variable describes change, while final_mm describes size. These answer different questions. Always say which you are comparing.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 8 — Turn measurements into a useful figure
text:
Select observations and variables

control_plants <- filter(seedlings, treatment == "control")
growth_table <- select(seedlings, plant_id, treatment, growth_mm)

filter() selects rows satisfying a condition. == asks whether values are equal; it does not assign values. Quotation marks mark the text label "control". select() chooses columns. Neither operation changes the original raw CSV. Inspect control_plants: it should have twelve rows. growth_table should have 24 rows and three columns.
Sometimes it is easier to read a sequence from left to right:

longer_control <- seedlings |>
  filter(treatment == "control") |>
  filter(growth_mm > 15)

The base R pipe |> passes the result on its left as the first argument to the next function. Read this as “take seedlings, keep controls, then keep growth over 15 mm”. This is a convenience for joining steps, not a new biological operation. Run intermediate steps when diagnosing a problem.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 8 — Turn measurements into a useful figure
text:
Map columns to a figure

size_plot <- ggplot(seedlings, aes(x = initial_mm, y = final_mm,
                                  colour = treatment)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Initial seedling length (mm)",
       y = "Final seedling length (mm)",
       colour = "Treatment") +
  theme_minimal()
size_plot

ggplot() identifies the table. aes() maps columns to positions and colour. Each point is one plant. The + adds a layer or a display instruction to the figure. The plus at the end of a line tells R that the expression continues. Colour maps a group label; it does not mean the treatment is a numeric measurement.
Read the labels before interpreting the pattern. The horizontal axis is initial length, so this figure does not directly show growth. It also cannot by itself prove that starting longer causes a larger final length.

growth_plot <- ggplot(seedlings, aes(x = treatment, y = growth_mm)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0, seed = 8),
             alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Treatment", y = "Change in seedling length (mm)") +
  theme_minimal()
growth_plot

This shows growth for each group. A small horizontal jitter separates points that would overlap; height = 0 leaves every measured vertical value unchanged. seed = 8 makes this display repeatable. No test is needed today: describe what you can see, including overlap and variation among plants.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 8 — Turn measurements into a useful figure
section: Save something another application can read
text:
Save something another application can read



The worked figure shows individual seedling growth measurements by treatment; the groups overlap.



ggsave("output/seedling-growth.png", plot = growth_plot,
       width = 6, height = 4, dpi = 150)
write_csv(growth_table, "output/seedling-growth.csv")

The supplied project includes output/. These commands create files there; they may replace files with the same names. The plot object in memory and the PNG on disk are different things. Locate and open both saved outputs in the file manager.

title: Day 8 — Turn measurements into a useful figure
text:
Your practical

Recreate both plots from the start of the script and calculate P02’s growth by hand to check the subtraction.
Save a table containing only treated plants’ IDs and growth measurements.
Choose one transfer task: make a plot of initial length against growth with axes labelled in mm, or adapt the same workflow to the organic-product table below. Do one, not both.
Write two sentences: one describing a visible pattern, one identifying a question the plot alone cannot settle.
Restart R and run the script. Confirm the saved files still open afterwards.


Alternative transfer task: a derived yield column
Our simulated table data/organic-recovery.csv records twelve separate runs of an organic synthesis, six assigned to each of two protocols, standard and modified. A run is one independently performed preparation. These labels identify procedures; you do not need to know their chemical steps.
Each row supplies a theoretical_mass_g: the maximum product mass from that run’s starting materials. isolated_mass_g is collected dry product, assumed pure for this simplified exercise. Both are grams. Calculate yield_percent = 100 × isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g. You are given the maximum and do not need to derive it from a reaction. The first run, Y01, has 1.00 g maximum and 0.62 g collected, so its yield is 62%.

organic <- read_csv("data/organic-recovery.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
organic <- mutate(organic,
                  yield_percent = 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g)
head(organic)

The runs started at different scales, so larger collected mass alone need not mean a greater yield. Inspect the supplied dictionary in data/README.md. Make a plot with protocol on x and percentage yield on y, using the familiar individual-point pattern. Label its y-axis “Isolated product yield (%)”. Save the derived table to output/organic-yields.csv and your plot to output/organic-yields.png. Keep its import and calculation in day08.R.






Hint: adapt the roles, not just the title





Use organic as the plot’s data, protocol for x, and yield_percent for y. Choose horizontal jitter with zero vertical jitter as above. Use write_csv() for the derived table and ggsave() for the figure. Expect 12 rows, no missing masses, and Y01 at 62%. A plot shows these results; it does not establish that one protocol is generally better or that a higher yield means purer product.









Hint: a plot or file is missing





Printing growth_plot shows the plot; assigning it alone may not. Check getwd() and dir.exists("output") if saving fails. If a column is not found, check names(seedlings) and run the earlier mutate() line.

title: Day 8 — Turn measurements into a useful figure
text:
Check your understanding






Why keep the raw table?





A derived table lets someone trace the calculation back to the recorded lengths. P02 grew 8.0 mm. Selecting columns is not selecting plants; select() and filter() act on different parts of the table.



Keep: day08.R, your derived tables, and figures in output/. If you chose the organic transfer, its two organic-yields outputs replace the extra initial-length-versus-growth figure; retain the main seedling work. Next: put explanation and code in one report.

title: Day 10 — A first biological report
text:
What a reader needs
A reader who was not in the room needs to know the question, what was measured, how you calculated the result, and what the figure shows. A list of function calls is not a methods explanation. “We calculated change in length as final minus initial length for each plant” explains the calculation in biological terms. The code makes the calculation repeatable.
The supplied experiment has 24 independently potted seedlings, twelve randomly assigned to each group. Initial and final measurements come from the same plant, seven days apart. The treatment label treated denotes a nutrient treatment; the nutrient formulation is unspecified. Do not invent details beyond the dictionary. These are simulated measurements.
Start with the familiar analysis:

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
seedlings <- mutate(seedlings, growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)

Put these lines in a code chunk before any result that depends on them. Give the reader a few simple checks:

nrow(seedlings)
sum(is.na(seedlings$growth_mm))
range(seedlings$growth_mm)

The file has 24 plants and no missing growth values. The minimum and maximum are measurements, not plausible bounds for every seedling in nature. The range summarises this dataset; it is sensitive to unusual observations.
crumbs: Week 2: R and a first report

title: Day 10 — A first biological report
text:
A figure worth discussing
Recreate the plot of growth against treatment from day 8. Show every plant, label the growth axis in mm, and explain that each dot represents one independently potted plant. Include the caption and discuss the visible overlap between groups.

Avoid declaring that a treatment “works” on the strength of a higher-looking cloud of points. We have not yet considered how much uncertainty surrounds a group comparison.

title: Day 12 — An average does not describe every plant
text: Two groups can have the same average growth yet look very different. How can we say where measurements are centred and how much individual plants vary? Today we use small numbers first, then connect them to the seedling experiment.

title: Day 12 — An average does not describe every plant
section: Mean and median answer slightly different questions
text:
Mean and median answer slightly different questions
The mean adds all observed values and divides by their number. The median is the middle of the ordered values, or the mean of the middle two for an even number of values. Both describe a centre; neither replaces the observations.

growth_mm <- c(12, 14, 16)
mean(growth_mm)
median(growth_mm)

Both results are 14 mm. Now inspect a more uneven set:

uneven_mm <- c(10, 10, 10, 100)
mean(uneven_mm)
median(uneven_mm)

The mean is 32.5 mm and median 10 mm. Neither is an arithmetic error. The large observation affects the mean strongly. Investigate whether a large value is supported by the source record; do not delete it simply to make the mean and median agree. The appropriate description depends on the question and shape of the measurements.

title: Day 12 — An average does not describe every plant
section: Variance measures spread around the mean
text:
Variance measures spread around the mean
For the three measurements 12, 14, and 16 mm, the deviations from their mean are −2, 0, and 2 mm. Their sum is zero, so an ordinary mean deviation would hide the spread. Squaring deviations prevents positive and negative values cancelling.
The sample variance adds squared deviations and divides by one less than the number of observations. The choice of this denominator helps estimate population variance from a sample; a derivation is beyond this course.

growth_mm <- c(12, 14, 16)
deviations_mm <- growth_mm - mean(growth_mm)
squared_deviations <- deviations_mm^2
sum(squared_deviations) / (length(growth_mm) - 1)
var(growth_mm)
sd(growth_mm)

The squared deviations are 4, 0, and 4. Their sum divided by 2 is 4 mm², the sample variance. The standard deviation, or SD, is its square root: 2 mm. SD is expressed in the original measurement’s units, which makes it easier to interpret alongside the mean. Variance uses squared units. Neither is the error in the mean or a claim that every plant lies within one SD.

close_mm <- c(13, 14, 15)
spread_mm <- c(8, 14, 20)
mean(close_mm)
mean(spread_mm)
sd(close_mm)
sd(spread_mm)

Both means are 14 mm. The SDs are 1 and 6 mm. The second set varies more among observations. A group with larger spread is not automatically measured less carefully: organisms can really differ. Measurement noise and biological variation can both contribute to observed spread.



Two toy groups share a mean of 14 mm but differ in spread. Dots are measurements; the dashed line is their common mean.

title: Day 12 — An average does not describe every plant
text:
Apply the descriptions to plants
Use the clean supplied table today so that variation is not confused with the repair exercise. Recreate all prerequisites in day12-variation.R.

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
control <- filter(seedlings, treatment == "control")
mean(control$growth_mm)
median(control$growth_mm)
var(control$growth_mm)
sd(control$growth_mm)

The control mean is about 15.3 mm and its SD about 3.19 mm. Report them with units and a sensible number of decimals; extra decimal places do not create more precise measurements. R may display more digits to help calculation, but those are not a requirement for prose.

title: Day 12 — An average does not describe every plant
section: Transfer choice: variation in collected product
text:
Transfer choice: variation in collected product
An organic synthesis is an experiment intended to make a product. In our simulated data/organic-recovery.csv, each row is one independent run. The supplied theoretical mass is the maximum product mass possible from that run’s starting materials; you do not need to derive it. Isolated mass is the dry product actually collected, assumed pure for this simplified calculation. Both are in grams. Calculate percentage yield as 100 × isolated mass / theoretical mass.

organic <- read_csv("data/organic-recovery.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(yield_percent = 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g)
standard_runs <- filter(organic, protocol == "standard")
mean(standard_runs$yield_percent)
var(standard_runs$yield_percent)
sd(standard_runs$yield_percent)

Y01 gives 100 × 0.62 / 1.00 = 62%. For the six standard-protocol runs, the mean is about 68.67%, variance 18.67 squared percentage points, and SD 4.32 percentage points. A difference from 62% to 70% is eight percentage points, not an eight-percent relative increase. Repeat the summaries for the modified protocol and describe centre and spread in two sentences.
The runs used different starting amounts, so raw collected grams do not make the same comparison as percentage yield. A higher yield alone does not establish greater purity or a generally better method. Save this calculation in today’s script; no knowledge of reaction mechanisms is needed.






Hint: use the units to check yourself





Adding a constant shifts the centre but leaves deviations unchanged. Dividing lengths by ten divides the mean and SD by ten, but divides variance by one hundred. Check ?var and ?sd for the functions’ definitions and missing-value arguments.

title: Day 12 — An average does not describe every plant
text:
Check your understanding






Which spread is larger?





The treated SD is about 4.87 mm, larger than the control SD. This describes variation among these plants; it does not by itself quantify uncertainty in the difference between group means. We will separate those questions next.

title: Day 14 — More readings are not always more independent evidence
text: Would measuring the same plant ten times tell us as much about other plants as measuring ten different plants? The answer changes how we count evidence and interpret an average. Today is about experimental reasoning, supported by a small simulation provided for you to run. You do not need to write simulations.

title: Day 14 — More readings are not always more independent evidence
section: Identify what was independently sampled or treated
text:
Identify what was independently sampled or treated
In the seedling experiment, plants are grown in separate pots and treatment is randomly assigned to plants. The plant is our independent experimental unit. An independent biological replicate provides another unit relevant to the question. A technical replicate repeats measurement of the same material, helping reveal measurement variation.
Three ruler readings of P01 can help assess how consistently it was measured. They do not turn it into three independently treated plants. Similarly, 100 cells from one organism are not automatically 100 independent organisms, and ten time points from one culture are not ten independent cultures. The unit follows the design and biological question, not the number of rows in a spreadsheet.
Imagine a nutrient treatment assigned to two trays, each holding twelve plants. If each tray receives a single shared treatment, the tray is a treatment unit. Treating all 24 plants as independently randomised units would overstate the independent treatment information. More data rows cannot repair that design.

title: Day 14 — More readings are not always more independent evidence
section: Spread among plants versus uncertainty in a mean
text:
Spread among plants versus uncertainty in a mean
SD describes how much measured plants vary. Sampling uncertainty concerns how our estimated mean would change if we repeated the sampling process. Even when a population’s spread stays the same, a mean based on more independent plants typically varies less from sample to sample.
Here is a teacher-provided demonstration. The clean seedling growth measurements serve as a fixed toy population for repeated sampling. This is not a new experiment and is not evidence about all plants in nature. Sampling with replacement is used to illustrate repeated draws from a fixed distribution.
Save the block in day14-sampling.R, then run it unchanged first:

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
population_mm <- seedlings$growth_mm
set.seed(14)
means_4 <- replicate(400, mean(sample(population_mm, size = 4, replace = TRUE)))
means_16 <- replicate(400, mean(sample(population_mm, size = 16, replace = TRUE)))
sampling <- data.frame(mean_mm = c(means_4, means_16),
                       sample_size = rep(c("4 plants", "16 plants"), each = 400))
ggplot(sampling, aes(x = mean_mm)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ sample_size, ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = "Mean growth in one simulated sample (mm)",
       y = "Number of simulated samples") +
  theme_minimal()
sd(population_mm)
sd(means_4)
sd(means_16)

sample() draws a sample; replicate() repeats the calculation 400 times. replace = TRUE allows a source value to be drawn more than once. set.seed() sets the starting state of the random-number generator so the demonstration can be repeated exactly. The resulting 400 means are summaries of simulated samples, not 400 newly measured plants.
Notice the horizontal axis: each value is a sample mean. Compare its spread between sample sizes. Do not confuse sd(means_16) with SD among the 16 plants inside one particular sample. The former describes variation among repeated estimates and approximates a standard error in this toy sampling process.

title: Day 14 — More readings are not always more independent evidence
text:
Your practical



Repeated sample means from samples of sixteen plants cluster more tightly than means from samples of four. The source distribution is fixed in this toy demonstration.



Before running the demonstration, predict which sample means will spread out more. Compare the plot and printed SDs with your prediction.
Change the random seed to 25 and rerun. Exact bins change; does the main relationship between sample size and spread remain?
Draw a small diagram for each design: twelve independent pots; one pot with twelve ruler readings; two trays with twelve plants each and tray-level treatment. Label the unit assigned to treatment. As an alternative to the one-pot diagram, draw one synthesis run whose collected product is weighed twelve times: there is one independently prepared run, not twelve. In the simulated organic dataset, six separately prepared runs were randomly assigned to each protocol; those runs provide independent protocol units.
Write an explanation for a lab partner: “We have many measurements, but our number of independently treated units is …”. Complete it for each design.
Save a two-sentence explanation of the difference between SD among plants and uncertainty in a group mean for your report.







Hint: keep the sampling target fixed





Both means_4 and means_16 draw from the same population_mm. A larger sample does not alter those source values or their SD. It changes how much the repeated sample means vary. These combined-treatment values are only a teaching population; this simulation is not a treatment comparison.

title: Day 14 — More readings are not always more independent evidence
text:
Check your understanding






Is a precise mean enough?





No. Repeated measurements may be biased, dependent, or drawn from an unrepresentative source. A narrow sampling distribution does not establish that the sampling process answers the intended biological question. Independent units and an appropriate design still matter.

title: Day 16 — What does a difference between groups mean?
text:
Does the treatment change how much a seedling grows? We already know how to describe the plants we measured. Today we distinguish a difference in our sample from evidence about a wider process. We begin with plants and pictures, then add statistical language. No new test is needed today.
Open introcomputing.Rproj. Use the clean, simulated data/seedlings.csv, not your data-repair exercise. Each row is one independently potted plant. Twelve plants were randomly assigned to each group and measured before and after the same growth period. The outcome is growth in millimetres. The treatment label describes an experimental condition; these teaching data do not establish a claim about any actual product or organism.

title: Day 16 — What does a difference between groups mean?
text:
Does the treatment change how much a seedling grows? We already know how to describe the plants we measured. Today we distinguish a difference in our sample from evidence about a wider process. We begin with plants and pictures, then add statistical language. No new test is needed today.
Open introcomputing.Rproj. Use the clean, simulated data/seedlings.csv, not your data-repair exercise. Each row is one independently potted plant. Twelve plants were randomly assigned to each group and measured before and after the same growth period. The outcome is growth in millimetres. The treatment label describes an experimental condition; these teaching data do not establish a claim about any actual product or organism.

title: Day 16 — What does a difference between groups mean?
section: Start with the question and the independent unit
text:
Start with the question and the independent unit
Our comparison is mean growth in treated plants minus mean growth in control plants. State that direction now: a positive difference means greater growth in the treated group. Keep it the same in your code and report.
The independent experimental unit is a plant in its own pot. Measuring one plant three times with a ruler may improve the measurement; it does not create three independent plants. Similarly, the initial and final measurements belong to the same plant. We subtract them to obtain one growth value per plant, then compare growth between the two independent treatment groups.

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
seedlings <- seedlings |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)

group_summary <- seedlings |>
  group_by(treatment) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_growth_mm = mean(growth_mm),
            sd_growth_mm = sd(growth_mm), .groups = "drop")
group_summary

The control mean is about 15.28 mm; the treated mean is about 21.49 mm. Both groups contain 12 plants. Their observed difference is about 6.22 mm. A difference is a number with units, not merely a label such as “significant”.

title: Day 16 — What does a difference between groups mean?
section: Show the observations before summarising the evidence
text:
Show the observations before summarising the evidence

growth_plot <- ggplot(seedlings, aes(x = treatment, y = growth_mm)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0, seed = 16)) +
  labs(x = "Treatment group", y = "Growth over the study period (mm)") +
  theme_minimal()
growth_plot




Individual growth values in the supplied simulated dataset. The slight horizontal displacement separates overlapping dots.


The small horizontal displacement separates overlapping dots. It does not change their heights. You can see variation among individuals and overlap between the groups. Overlap does not automatically mean that the group means are equal; separated means do not mean that every treated plant grew more than every control plant. Compare both statements against the picture.

title: Day 16 — What does a difference between groups mean?
section: A sample difference is not the whole story
text:
A sample difference is not the whole story
If we repeated the experiment with another set of plants, we would get another difference. Random variation can produce unequal sample means even when the underlying group means are equal. Tomorrow’s test asks whether the observed difference is difficult to reconcile with a particular equal-means model.
The null hypothesis for this exercise is that the population mean growth is the same under the two conditions. A two-sided alternative allows a difference in either direction. We choose a two-sided question before looking for the most favourable result.
A p-value describes how often a result at least as extreme as the one observed would arise under the null model and its assumptions. For the t-test, “extreme” refers to the test statistic, which compares the mean difference with its estimated sampling uncertainty. A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and it does not measure the biological importance of a difference.

title: Day 16 — What does a difference between groups mean?
text:
Practical: prepare a comparison report
Save a copy of the root-level report.Rmd as comparison.Rmd, also at the project root so its data/ paths work. Keep your earlier reports. In this new file:

Write the biological question, outcome units, and independent experimental unit.
Add the import, growth calculation, group summary, and individual-point plot.
Calculate the treated-minus-control difference with the following explicit extraction. pull() takes one column out of a table as a vector.


treated <- seedlings |>
  filter(treatment == "treated") |>
  pull(growth_mm)
control <- seedlings |>
  filter(treatment == "control") |>
  pull(growth_mm)

observed_difference <- mean(treated) - mean(control)
observed_difference


Write two sentences: one describes the sample difference, and one says what still remains uncertain about the wider population.
Save the figure with ggsave("output/day16-growth.png", growth_plot,    width = 6, height = 4) and render the report to HTML.







Hint: check a surprising sign





Read mean(treated) and mean(control) separately. The order in a subtraction matters. A negative result from mean(control) - mean(treated) would describe the reverse comparison, not a contradictory biological result.

title: Day 16 — What does a difference between groups mean?
text:
Check your understanding

Can we conclude that every treated plant grew more? No; look at the dots.
Are 12 plants each measured twice 24 independent replicates per group? No; repeated measurements stay attached to their plant.
Does an observed mean difference alone tell us its sampling uncertainty? No; variability and sample size matter as well.

Leave with: comparison.Rmd, its rendered HTML, and output/day16-growth.png. Your report should currently describe the observations without pretending that a test has already been performed.

title: Day 18 — The same plant measured twice
text:
Ten plants had their leaf photosynthesis measured before and after changing the light conditions. Did their measurements tend to increase? Every plant appears twice, so this is a paired design. We compare changes within plants rather than pretending that the two sets of readings came from different plants.
The file data/paired.csv contains simulated measurements in micromoles of CO2 per square metre per second, written µmol m⁻² s⁻¹. You do not need the chemistry to analyse this example: each number measures a rate, and higher means a greater rate of photosynthesis. Before and after were always measured in that order. That matters for our eventual interpretation.

We compare changes within plants rather than pretending that the two sets of readings came from different plants.

title: Day 18 — The same plant measured twice
section: Each row keeps a pair together
text:
Each row keeps a pair together

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

paired <- read_csv("data/paired.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
paired
anyDuplicated(paired$plant_id)

There should be ten rows and no duplicate identifiers; anyDuplicated() returns zero when it finds none. Each row contains one plant’s before and after values. The identifiers tell us which measurements belong together. If measurements came in two files, we would need to match them by identifier before subtracting. The fact that two files each contain ten rows would not be sufficient.
Never sort the before values and after values independently. That would change which values are paired and manufacture different biological changes. Sorting the complete table by plant identifier is safe because whole rows move together.

title: Day 18 — The same plant measured twice
section: Make one change value per plant
text:
Make one change value per plant

paired <- paired |>
  mutate(change_umol_m2_s = after_umol_m2_s - before_umol_m2_s)

paired |>
  select(plant_id, before_umol_m2_s, after_umol_m2_s, change_umol_m2_s)

mean(paired$change_umol_m2_s)

Plant L01 changed from 5.87 to 6.95, an increase of 1.08 units. The mean of all ten changes is 1.983 units. Some plants start higher than others; analysing the within-plant changes recognises that each plant is its own reference.

change_plot <- ggplot(paired, aes(x = plant_id, y = change_umol_m2_s)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Plant identifier", y = "After − before (µmol m⁻² s⁻¹)") +
  theme_minimal()
change_plot




Each point is one plant’s after-minus-before change; the dashed line marks no change.


The zero line means no change. This plot makes the paired comparison visible without requiring another data-reshaping tool. Inspect the changes, including the larger change for L02; a valid large change must not be removed merely because it is inconvenient.

title: Day 18 — The same plant measured twice
section: A paired t-test asks about the mean change
text:
A paired t-test asks about the mean change

paired_comparison <- t.test(paired$after_umol_m2_s,
                            paired$before_umol_m2_s,
                            paired = TRUE,
                            alternative = "two.sided")
paired_comparison

Here the first vector is after and the second before. The mean difference is therefore after minus before. The estimated mean change is about 1.98, with a 95% confidence interval from 1.25 to 2.71 units and p about 0.00017. The method describes uncertainty in the mean change, not the spread of individual changes. Its independent observations are the ten plants’ changes.
A paired t-test can also be understood as a one-sample t-test of the change values against zero. Try the following only after you can explain the first version; it should give the same estimated change, interval, and p-value:

t.test(paired$change_umol_m2_s, mu = 0)

title: Day 18 — The same plant measured twice
section: What this experiment can and cannot show
text:
What this experiment can and cannot show
The readings increased in this simulated dataset. But light condition and measurement order changed together. Time, acclimation, or equipment drift could also contribute. A small p-value does not untangle these possibilities. We can describe a before–after association and propose a better experiment, such as an appropriate control group and a design that addresses order effects.
This illustrates two different questions: are the observed changes consistent with a zero mean change, and what caused any change? A test addresses the first under assumptions; the experimental design determines what we can say about the second.

title: Day 18 — The same plant measured twice
text:
Practical: a short paired report
Copy the root report template to paired-report.Rmd at the project root. Include:

The question, units, and ten independent plants measured twice.
An import and ID check, the change calculation, and the change plot.
The paired t-test and an interpretation in the stated after-minus-before direction.
One sentence distinguishing the confidence interval from individual spread.
A limitation about order and an idea for improving the design.

Save change_plot as output/day18-changes.png and render the HTML. All the measurements are complete here. In real paired data, do not remove missing before and after values independently, since that can misalign the remaining pairs. Keep rows together and account for any incomplete pairs explicitly.






Hint: check the direction with one plant





Before trusting the test output, subtract L01’s before value from its after value. It should be positive 1.08. The same order belongs in both the change calculation and the two vectors supplied to t.test().

title: Day 18 — The same plant measured twice
text:
Check your understanding

How many independent units are present? Ten plants, not twenty readings.
Would pairing unrelated plants by their row position be meaningful? No.
Does a small p-value establish that light caused the change? No; the fixed measurement order remains a limitation.
